‘So there really are such beauties in the world!’ she said, smiling. ‘I had never seen one till today. And with that bearing, you would never take her for your daughter’s child, Grandmother. She looks like your own son’s daughter. No wonder you think and talk of her all day long.

‘Only it’s so pitiful that this dear little cousin should have such a hard lot. Why did Aunt have to die?’ She wiped her eyes with her handkerchief.
‘I had only just stopped, and here you are setting me off again,’ Grandmother Jia said with a smile. ‘Your cousin has had a long journey, and she’s frail too. We had only just consoled her. Now, no more about that!’
Xi-feng immediately changed from sorrow to cheerfulness.
‘Of course! The moment I saw her, I could think of nothing else. I was so glad and so sad that I quite forgot you, Grandmother. I deserve a good beating!’
She took Dai-yu’s hand again. ‘How old are you, my dear? Have you been to lessons? What medicine are you taking? You mustn’t pine for home here. If there’s anything you’d like to eat or play with, just tell me. And if the maids or old women don’t behave, tell me that too.’
She turned to the women servants. ‘Has Miss Lin’s luggage been brought in? How many people came with her? Get two rooms in the servants’ quarters cleaned up at once, and let them have a rest.’

While they were talking, tea and fruit had been laid out. Xi-feng herself presented Dai-yu with both. Dai-yu then heard her second aunt ask Xi-feng, ‘Have the monthly allowances been paid?’
‘They’ve all been paid. I was just taking some people up to the back storey to look for satin. We hunted for ages and couldn’t find the kind you mentioned yesterday. Perhaps you remembered it wrongly, ma’am?’
‘It hardly matters whether there is any,’ Lady Wang said. Then she added, ‘You should have taken out a couple of lengths while you were there, to make clothes for your cousin. Remind me this evening to have someone fetch them. Don’t forget.’
‘I had thought of that already,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Knowing she was due any day now, I’ve set some aside. Once you’ve been back and seen them, I can send them over.’
Lady Wang smiled and nodded without speaking.

When the tea and fruit had been cleared away, Grandmother Jia told two old nurses to take Dai-yu to pay her respects to her two maternal uncles. Jia She’s wife, Lady Xing, rose too.
‘It would be convenient for me to take my niece over,’ she said with a smile.
‘Yes, do go,’ Grandmother Jia replied, smiling. ‘You needn’t come back here.’
Lady Xing answered, ‘Yes,’ and took Dai-yu to say goodbye to Lady Wang. Everyone accompanied them as far as the passage-hall. Outside the flower-carved gate the young servants had already brought up a carriage with green curtains and a blue silk cover. Lady Xing took Dai-yu inside. The women lowered the curtains before ordering the young servants to lift and draw it to a wider space, where a docile mule was harnessed to it. They too went out through the small western gate, turned east past the main entrance of the Rong mansion and entered a great black-lacquered gateway, stopping before the ceremonial inner gate. Only after the young servants had withdrawn were the carriage curtains raised. Holding Dai-yu by the hand, Lady Xing led her into the courtyard. From the arrangement of the buildings and courtyards, Dai-yu judged that this must have been partitioned off from the Rong mansion’s garden.

After they had passed through three ceremonial gates, she found that the main rooms, side rooms and covered walks were all small and finely arranged, quite unlike the lofty splendour of the apartments she had just left. Trees and ornamental rocks stood everywhere in the courtyard. They entered the principal room, where a number of concubines and maids in splendid dress came to meet them. Lady Xing asked Dai-yu to sit down and sent someone to fetch Jia She from the outer study. Presently the messenger returned.
‘His Lordship says, “I have been unwell for several days. Seeing the young lady would only grieve us both, and for the moment I cannot bear it. Tell her not to be sad or homesick. With her grandmother and her aunts, it will be just as though she were at home. Her cousins may be dull girls, but their company will help to relieve her loneliness. If anything troubles her, she must say so, and not treat us as strangers.”’
Dai-yu stood up quickly and listened to the whole message. After sitting a little longer, she asked leave to go.

Lady Xing pressed her to stay for supper, but Dai-yu replied with a smile, ‘It is very kind of you to offer me supper, Aunt, and I ought not to refuse. But I have still to pay my respects to my second uncle. I am afraid it would be discourteous to go only after I had eaten. May I accept your kindness another day? I hope you will forgive me.’
‘Of course,’ Lady Xing said, smiling.

She instructed two or three nurses to take good care of the young lady and escort her back in the same carriage. Dai-yu took her leave. Lady Xing saw her as far as the ceremonial gate, gave the servants a few more instructions, and watched the carriage go before returning inside.

Soon Dai-yu was back at the Rong mansion and alighted from the carriage. The nurses led her round to the east, through an east–west passage-hall, to a large courtyard inside the ceremonial gate behind the great south-facing hall. The principal building had five bays. Side rooms and low-roofed annexes joined it through the gables, with passages leading in every direction. Its imposing magnificence was quite different from Grandmother Jia’s apartments. Dai-yu recognised this as the principal inner residence. A broad paved walk led straight out to the main gate. On entering the hall, the first thing she saw when she looked up was a great blue tablet bearing nine dragons in gold. Three enormous characters read ‘Rong-xi Hall’. A small inscription behind them said, ‘Written and bestowed upon Jia Yuan, Duke of Rong, on such-and-such a day, month and year’, followed by the imperial seal, ‘Treasure of the Imperial Brush Amid Myriad Affairs’. On a great rosewood table carved with hornless dragons stood an ancient bronze tripod, some three chi high, with a blue-green patina. Above hung a large ink painting of a dragon, entitled ‘Awaiting the Water-clock to Attend Court’. On one side was a golden ape-shaped ritual vessel; on the other, a large glass drinking vessel. Below, sixteen nanmu folding chairs stood in two rows. A couplet, its engraved silver characters inlaid in ebony boards, read:
Pearls and jewels upon these seats shine with the sun and moon;
Robes of office before this hall set cloud and mist ablaze.

Below, in smaller characters, was written: ‘Respectfully inscribed by Mu Shi, hereditary Prince of Dong’an, a junior fellow countryman bound to you by generations of family friendship.’ Lady Wang did not ordinarily sit or rest in this main hall, but in the three-bay suite to its east. The old nurses now led Dai-yu through the eastern doorway. The great kang beneath the window was covered with a scarlet foreign woollen rug. A scarlet backrest with a pattern of coin-roundels and mang dragons stood against the wall, with dark-blue bolsters and a long olive-yellow mattress in the same design. On either side was a little plum-blossom-shaped table in foreign lacquer. On the left stood a King Wen-style tripod incense burner, with its spoon, tongs and incense box; on the right a slender ‘beauty’ vase of Ru ware, filled with flowers in season, as well as tea bowls, a spittoon and other things. Four chairs faced west below the kang, each draped in a pink floral cover, with four footstools beneath. A pair of tall stands flanked the chairs, also furnished with tea bowls and vases of flowers.

There is no need to describe the remaining furnishings in detail. The old nurses invited Dai-yu to sit on the kang. But there were two brocade cushions set opposite one another along its edge, and, judging the precedence of the places, she declined to mount it and sat instead on a chair to the east. The maids of these apartments hurried to bring tea. As Dai-yu drank, she observed their clothes and ornaments, their bearing and movements. They too were indeed unlike the servants of other households.

Before she had finished her tea, a maid in a red silk-twill jacket and a blue satin waistcoat with piped edges came in, smiling.
‘Her Ladyship asks Miss Lin to come and sit in the other room.’
The nurses led Dai-yu out and into a small three-bay range off the eastern covered walk. A low table stood across the kang in the main room, piled with books and tea things. Against the eastern wall, facing west, were a somewhat worn blue satin backrest and bolsters. Lady Wang sat at the lower place to the west, on a cushion with a backrest of the same worn blue satin. Seeing Dai-yu, she invited her to take the eastern place. Dai-yu felt certain that this was Jia Zheng’s seat. Beside the kang she noticed a row of three chairs draped with somewhat worn

covers patterned with splashes of ink, and sat on one of these instead. Only after Lady Wang had repeatedly taken her hand and urged her up onto the kang did she sit beside her.
‘Your uncle has gone to observe a fast today,’ Lady Wang said. ‘You can see him another time. There is just one thing I must tell you. Your three girl cousins are all very good. You will study, learn your characters and do needlework together, and if you sometimes play or joke, they will always give way to you. But there is one thing that worries me greatly. I have a son who is the very root of mischief, born to cause trouble,

‘the “Demon King” of this household. He went to the temple today to fulfil a vow and is not back yet. You’ll understand when you see him this evening. From now on you must take no notice of him. None of your girl cousins dares to provoke him.’

Dai-yu had often heard her mother speak of a boy cousin, the son of her second aunt, who had been born with a piece of jade in his mouth. He was extraordinarily unruly, hated studying, and liked nothing better than to spend his time among the women and girls. His grandmother doted on him, and no one dared discipline him. From Lady Wang’s words Dai-yu knew that this must be the cousin she meant.
She smiled politely. ‘Do you mean the cousin who was born with the jade, Aunt? At home I often heard Mother speak of him. She said he was a year older than me and his childhood name was Bao-yu; although he was very wilful and mischievous, he was wonderfully affectionate towards his sisters and girl cousins. Now that I am here, I shall naturally be with the girls. The boys have their own rooms in another courtyard. How could I have occasion to provoke him?’
‘You don’t understand,’ Lady Wang said, smiling. ‘He is not like other boys. From his earliest years your grandmother has spoilt him, bringing him up with the girls, and he is used to being indulged among them. On a day when they pay him no attention, he is rather quieter. Even if he feels neglected, he only goes outside the inner gate and takes it out on his two little pages where no one can see. A little muttering, and it is over.

‘But if the girls say one word more than usual to him that day, he is so pleased with himself that there is no end to the trouble he makes. That is why I am telling you to take no notice of him. One moment he is all honeyed words, the next he acknowledges neither heaven nor authority, and the next he talks like a madman or an idiot. Just don’t believe him.’

Dai-yu agreed to each of these instructions. A maid then came to announce, ‘Supper is being served at Her Old Ladyship’s.’
Lady Wang at once took Dai-yu through the rear doorway, west along the covered walk and out through a side gate into a broad north–south passage between walls. To the south stood a small three-bay hall, its back towards the outer approach, with a projecting covered porch; to the north was a great screen wall painted white. Behind it were a smallish gateway and a small set of rooms.
Lady Wang pointed them out with a smile. ‘Those are your Cousin Feng’s rooms. You can come and find her here later. Whatever you need, just tell her.’
Four or five young servants, still with their hair tied in little children’s tufts, stood by the courtyard gate with their hands at their sides. Lady Wang led Dai-yu through another east–west passage-hall into Grandmother Jia’s rear courtyard. They entered by the back door, where many attendants were already waiting. Only when Lady Wang arrived were the table and chairs set in place. Jia Zhu’s wife, née Li, brought the rice; Xi-feng laid out the chopsticks; Lady Wang presented the soup.

Grandmother Jia sat alone on the couch facing the room, with four empty chairs, two on either side. Xi-feng hurried to draw Dai-yu to the first chair on the left, but Dai-yu was most reluctant to accept it.
‘Your aunts and your cousins’ wives don’t eat here,’ Grandmother Jia said, smiling. ‘You are our guest. That is where you ought to sit.’
Only then did Dai-yu ask leave to be seated and sit down. Grandmother Jia told Lady Wang to sit. Ying-chun and the other two girls likewise asked leave before coming forward. Ying-chun took the first chair on the right, Tan-chun the second on the left, and Xi-chun the second on the right. Maids stood beside them holding fly-whisks, rinsing bowls and towels. Li and Xi-feng stood by the table, serving and inviting them to eat. Though many women servants and maids waited in the outer room, not so much as a cough was heard. The meal ended in silence. Maids brought each of them tea on small trays. Lin Ru-hai had taught his daughter to cherish her good fortune and preserve her health: after a meal she must be sure that every grain of rice had been swallowed and wait a while before drinking tea, so as not to harm the digestion. But Dai-yu had already seen many things here that differed from the customs at home and that she would have to follow. She must change her ways one by one. Accordingly she accepted the tea.

Someone promptly brought a rinsing bowl, and Dai-yu followed the others in rinsing her mouth. After they had washed their hands, more tea was brought. This was the tea for drinking.
‘You may go now,’ Grandmother Jia said. ‘Let us talk at our ease.’
Lady Wang rose at once. After a few more casual remarks she took Xi-feng and Li away. Grandmother Jia asked Dai-yu what she was studying.

‘I have only just been studying the Four Books,’ Dai-yu said. She then asked what her cousins were reading.
‘Reading?’ said Grandmother Jia. ‘They only learn a few characters, so that they won’t be blind with their eyes open!’

She had scarcely finished when footsteps sounded outside. A maid came in, smiling.
‘Bao-yu is here!’
Dai-yu was wondering, ‘What sort of idle scamp is this Bao-yu? What sort of muddle-headed, naughty child?’

She would have been quite content not to meet the stupid creature at all. Before the maid had finished announcing him, however, a young gentleman had entered. His hair was held by a coronet of reddish gold set with gems; level with his brows lay a golden band worked with two dragons contending for a pearl. He wore a scarlet, tight-sleeved robe patterned in two shades of gold with a hundred butterflies among flowers, a palace sash of five-coloured silk tied in flower-knots with long tassels, and over it a dark-blue Japanese-satin coat with eight roundels in raised weave and a fringe of tassels. On his feet were little court boots of blue satin with white soles. His face was like the mid-autumn moon, his colour like a flower at spring dawn. The hair at his temples was trimmed as if with a knife, his brows drawn in ink; his cheeks were peach petals, his eyes autumn waters. Even in anger he would seem to smile; even a reproachful glance would hold affection. About his neck was a gold circlet of hornless dragons, and on a cord of five-coloured silk hung a beautiful piece of jade.
Dai-yu was astonished at the sight of him. ‘How strange! It is as though I have seen him somewhere before. How can he look so familiar?’
Bao-yu greeted Grandmother Jia. ‘Go and see your mother,’ she told him, and he turned and went out.

When he returned a little later, he had changed his clothes and headgear. The short hair round his head was plaited into little braids tied with red silk, all gathered into the lock left to grow from infancy at the crown, and woven into a single long plait, black and shining as lacquer. A row of four large pearls ran from crown to tip, with a golden Eight Treasures ornament hanging at the end. He wore a somewhat worn pink long jacket scattered with flowers, and still had on his neck circlet, jade, the lock marking his dedication to a religious guardian, his protective charms and the rest. Below showed part of his pine-pollen-green flowered silk-twill trousers, ink-splashed stockings edged with brocade, and thick-soled scarlet shoes. His face looked more than ever as if it had been powdered, his lips as though touched with rouge. Affection moved in his glances; laughter was never far from his speech. All his natural charm was gathered in the tips of his brows, a lifetime’s countless feelings crowded into the corners of his eyes. His appearance was certainly superb, but what lay beneath it was harder to know. A later writer composed two lyrics to the tune ‘Moon over the West River’ which judged Bao-yu very aptly:

For no reason he seeks grief and resentment;
At times he seems an idiot, at times mad.
Granted, he was born with a handsome skin:
Inside, nothing grows but weeds.

Good for nothing, ignorant of worldly business,
Stupid and stubborn, afraid to study books;
Wayward in conduct, perverse in disposition,
What does he care for the world’s slander?

In wealth and honour he takes no joy in his proper work;
In poverty he could not bear the desolation.
Alas, he wastes the best years of his life:
Neither state nor family can hope for anything from him.

First under heaven for incompetence,
Without an equal, past or present, in unworthiness.
A word to you, sons of silk and rich food:
Do not model yourselves on this boy!

‘Nonsense again!’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘When could you ever have met her?’
Bao-yu smiled. ‘Even if I have never met her, her face is familiar. In my heart she counts as an old acquaintance. Why shouldn’t we treat today as a meeting after a long separation?’
‘Better still! Better still!’ Grandmother Jia said, laughing. ‘Then you will get on all the better.’
Bao-yu moved over to sit beside Dai-yu and studied her again.
‘Have you done any reading, Cousin?’
‘No,’ Dai-yu said. ‘I only went to lessons for a year. I know a few characters, that’s all.’
‘What are the two characters of your name?’
Dai-yu told him. He asked her courtesy name.
‘I haven’t one.’

‘Let me give you a wonderful one,’ Bao-yu said, smiling. ‘Nothing could be better than Pin-pin, “Frown-frown”.’
Tan-chun asked where he had found it.
‘The Comprehensive Survey of Persons Past and Present says, “In the west is a stone called dai, which can be used instead of ink for painting eyebrows.” And Cousin Lin’s brows look as though they are drawn together in a frown. Don’t those two characters make it doubly apt?’
‘I’m afraid you’ve made that up again,’ Tan-chun said, laughing.
Bao-yu laughed too. ‘Apart from the Four Books, there’s plenty that’s made up. Why am I the only one accused of inventing things?’
He asked Dai-yu another question. ‘Have you a jade too?’

No one understood what he meant. Dai-yu considered: ‘He has a jade himself, so he wants to know if I have one.’
‘I haven’t anything like that,’ she answered. ‘It must be something very rare. How could everyone have one?’
At this Bao-yu instantly flew into one of his fits of madness. He tore off the jade and flung it down with all his strength.
‘What’s rare about it?’ he cried angrily. ‘It can’t even tell the better people from the worse, and they call it “spiritual”! Spiritual indeed! I don’t want the wretched thing!’
Everyone rushed in alarm to pick it up. Grandmother Jia clasped him to her in great distress.
‘You wicked boy!

‘If you’re angry, you can easily hit someone or scold them. Why must you throw away your very life?’
Bao-yu sobbed, his face streaked with tears. ‘None of the girls at home has one. I’m the only one, and I said it was no fun. Now this cousin has come, lovely as an immortal, and she hasn’t one either. That proves it’s no good.’
Grandmother Jia hurried to soothe him. ‘Your cousin did have one. But when your aunt died, she couldn’t bear to leave her little girl, and there was nothing else to be done, so she took your cousin’s jade with her. It served as a burial offering, to express your cousin’s devotion, and it let your aunt’s spirit feel that she could still see her daughter. That’s why your cousin says she hasn’t one. She doesn’t like to boast about herself. How can you compare yourself with her now? Put it on again and take good care of it. Mind your mother doesn’t hear of this!’
She took the jade from a maid and put it back on him herself. Bao-yu thought this explanation made excellent sense and raised no further objections. Just then Dai-yu’s nurse came to ask where she was to sleep.

‘For now, move Bao-yu out to the warm side-room with me,’ Grandmother Jia said, ‘and put Miss Lin inside the gauze-screened alcove. Once the rest of the winter is over, we can get rooms ready for them in the spring and make fresh arrangements.’
‘Dearest Grandmother,’ Bao-yu said, ‘I shall be perfectly comfortable on the bed outside the gauze screen. Why move me out to disturb your peace?’
Grandmother Jia considered. ‘Very well.’
Each child was to have a nurse and a maid in attendance, with the others keeping watch in the outer room, ready to answer a call. Xi-feng had already sent over a flowered mauve bed-curtain, together with brocade quilts, satin mattresses and other bedding.

Dai-yu had brought only two attendants: Nurse Wang, who had nursed her from infancy, and a little maid of ten named Snowgoose, who had also been with her since she was very small. Grandmother Jia saw that Snowgoose was still thoroughly childish and Nurse Wang extremely old, and thought neither would be able to spare Dai-yu trouble or serve her as she wished. She therefore gave her one of her own second-ranking maids, called Ying-ge. In other respects Dai-yu was provided for on the same terms as Ying-chun and the others. Besides the nurse who had suckled each girl, there were four matrons to guide her conduct; besides the two personal maids who looked after her hair ornaments, washing and bathing, there were five or six little maids to sweep the rooms and run errands. Nurse Wang and Ying-ge now attended Dai-yu inside the green gauze screen. Outside, by the large bed, were Bao-yu’s wet-nurse, Nurse Li, and his senior maid, Aroma.

Aroma too had originally been Grandmother Jia’s maid, and her name had been Pearl. Doting on Bao-yu, Grandmother Jia had feared that none of his maids would give herself wholly to his service. She had always liked Aroma for her simple, good heart and the thoroughness with which she performed her duties, and had therefore given her to him. Bao-yu knew that her surname was Hua, ‘flower’, and had seen the phrase ‘the flowers’ aroma steals upon one’ in an old poem. He reported his wish to Grandmother Jia and changed her name to Aroma. Aroma had a certain single-mindedness of her own: when she served Grandmother Jia, the old lady alone filled her heart and eyes; now that she served Bao-yu, there was no one in her heart or eyes but Bao-yu. His perverse disposition, however, led her to remonstrate with him often and made her deeply anxious. That night, after Bao-yu and Nurse Li had gone to sleep, she saw that Dai-yu and Ying-ge were still awake inside. Having taken off her make-up, she slipped quietly in.
‘Why aren’t you resting yet, miss?’ she asked with a smile.
‘Please sit down, Sister,’ Dai-yu said at once.
Aroma sat on the edge of the bed.
‘Miss Lin has been upset,’ Ying-ge said, smiling. ‘She was crying and wiping her eyes, saying, “I had only just arrived, and already I brought on your young master’s madness. If he had broken the jade, wouldn’t it have been my fault?” That’s what was troubling her. I’ve only just managed to comfort her.’
‘Please don’t feel that way, miss,’ said Aroma. ‘You’ll probably see much stranger goings-on than that in future!

‘If you take his behaviour to heart and let it grieve you, I’m afraid there will be no end to your grieving. Please don’t fret over it!’
‘I shall remember what you both tell me,’ Dai-yu said. ‘But where did that jade come from, after all? Does it have writing on it?’
‘No one in the family knows where it came from,’ Aroma said. ‘There was already a hole in it. They say it was taken out of his mouth when he was born. Let me fetch it and you’ll see.’
Dai-yu stopped her at once. ‘No, never mind. It’s late now. Tomorrow will be soon enough.’
They talked a little longer, then at last went to bed.

Next morning, after getting up and paying her respects to Grandmother Jia, Dai-yu went to Lady Wang’s apartments. Lady Wang and Xi-feng were together, opening letters from Jinling. Two married women servants had also been sent with a message from Lady Wang’s brother and his wife. Dai-yu knew nothing of the circumstances, but Tan-chun and the others knew that they were discussing Xue Pan, their maternal cousin, the son of Aunt Xue in Jinling. Relying on his wealth and influence, he had beaten a man to death, and the case was now before the Yingtian prefecture. Their uncle Wang Zi-teng had heard the news and sent members of his household to tell Lady Wang’s family, with the intention of having the Xues called to the capital.

Now Dai-yu and the other girls went to Lady Wang’s rooms, where they found her discussing household business with a messenger from her brother and his wife. There was also talk of a homicide case involving the girls’ aunt’s family. Seeing how much Lady Wang had to attend to, they withdrew and went instead to the rooms of their widowed sister-in-law, Mrs Li.

This Mrs Li was Jia Zhu’s wife. Though Zhu had died young, he had fortunately left a son, Jia Lan, now just five years old and already attending school. Mrs Li too came from a distinguished official family of Jinling. Her father, Li Shou-zhong, had been Chancellor of the Imperial Academy, and there was not a man or woman in the clan who did not study books and recite poetry. Once Li Shou-zhong became head of the family, however, he maintained that ‘A woman’s virtue lies in having no accomplishments.’ When his daughter was born, therefore, he did not have her taught very much. Three or four works, such as the Four Books for Women, the Lives of Exemplary Women and the Collected Lives of Worthy Ladies, would suffice: she need only learn to recognise a few characters and remember a few virtuous women of earlier dynasties. Spinning and weaving, drawing water and pounding grain were what mattered. Accordingly, he named her Li Wan and gave her the courtesy name Gong-cai.

Thus Li Wan, though widowed in the bloom of youth and living amid fine food and silks, was like dead wood and cold ashes. She took notice of nothing, heard nothing, and knew only the service of her elders and the upbringing of her son. Beyond these duties, she kept her young sisters-in-law company at their needlework and reading. Though Dai-yu was a guest beneath another’s roof, she now had these girls with her every day. Apart from her elderly father, there was nothing more she need trouble about.

Let us turn for the moment to Yu-cun. He had been appointed to fill the vacant prefecture of Yingtian, and scarcely had he taken up his post when a report of a homicide came before him. Two families had tried to buy the same maid; neither would give way, and the quarrel had ended in a fatal beating. Yu-cun summoned the complainant for examination.

‘The man they beat to death was my master,’ the man said. ‘He bought a girl one day, never knowing she had been kidnapped and was being sold by her kidnapper. The fellow had already taken our money. Our young master said that the third day from then was an auspicious day, and he would wait till then to bring her home. But the kidnapper secretly sold her a second time, to the Xues. We found out and went to seize the seller and recover the girl. The Xues are one of the tyrants of Jinling. They used their power to intimidate us, and a gang of their brutal servants beat my young master to death. Both the murderer and his servants have fled without a trace. Only a few people who were not involved are left. I have been lodging complaints for a year, and no one will see justice done. I beg Your Honour to arrest the killers, root out these evil men and protect the widowed and the orphaned. The dead man’s gratitude for your boundless kindness would know no end!’
Yu-cun flew into a rage.
‘What damned nonsense is this? Beat a man to death and simply walk away, never to be caught?’

He was about to issue a warrant ordering his runners to arrest members of the murderer’s clan at once and question them under torture until they revealed where he was hiding. A general warrant for his arrest would also be circulated. Just as he was going to issue the order, however, an usher standing beside the tribunal desk caught his eye and signalled to him not to do so. Greatly puzzled, Yu-cun stayed his hand. He dismissed the court and retired to a private room, where he sent all his attendants away except the usher.
The man hurried forward to pay his respects.
‘Your Honour has been rising in rank and growing richer all this time,’ he said with a smile. ‘Have eight or nine years been enough to make you forget me?’
‘Your face is certainly very familiar. I simply cannot place you for the moment.’
The usher smiled. ‘Great men do have short memories, sir! Have you forgotten the very place you started from? Can you not remember the Gourd Temple?’

Yu-cun started as though struck by thunder. Only then did it come back to him. This usher had been a little novice in the Gourd Temple. After the fire he had had nowhere to live. He had thought of entering another temple to continue his religious life, but could not bear its bleak austerity. An usher’s work, he thought, would be lighter and offer more company and bustle. So, while still young enough, he had grown his hair again and taken up the occupation.
Yu-cun had never dreamed it could be he. He hastily took him by the hand and smiled.
‘An old friend, then!’
He invited him to sit down so that they could talk. The usher dared not accept.

‘One must never forget the friends of one’s poor days,’ Yu-cun said, smiling. ‘You and I are old friends. Besides, these are my private rooms. If we are to have a long talk, you cannot possibly remain standing.’
Only then did the usher thank him for the seat and perch sideways on its edge.
Yu-cun asked why he had signalled to stop the warrant.
‘Now that Your Honour has received this distinguished appointment in our province,’ the usher said, ‘surely you have had a copy made of the provincial “Charm for Protecting Officials”?’
‘What is this “Charm for Protecting Officials”?’ Yu-cun asked at once. ‘I know nothing of it.’
‘That will never do!’ said the usher.

‘How can you expect to last in office if you do not even know that? Every local official nowadays keeps a private list of the great gentry families in his province, the richest, noblest and most powerful of them all. It is the same in every province. If you do not know who they are and happen to offend one of them, you may lose more than your rank. You may not even keep your life. That is why we call it the “Charm for Protecting Officials”. How could Your Honour touch the Xues we have just been speaking of? There is nothing difficult about the case itself. It has dragged on like this only because no one wants to offend their connections.’
As he spoke, he took a handwritten copy of the charm from his pouch and handed it to Yu-cun. It consisted of popular sayings about the great local clans and families of high officials.

The sayings were neatly set out, each with notes below giving the rank and title of the family’s founding ancestor and the branches descended from him. The Stone once copied this list too. Here is what was written on it:

The Jias are no sham:
Their halls are white jade, their horses gold.

Three hundred li of Epang Palace
Cannot house the Shi clan of Jinling.

When the Eastern Sea lacks a white-jade bed,
The Dragon King comes to ask the Wangs of Jinling.

A splendid fall of snow for a year of plenty:
Pearls are dirt to them, and gold is iron.

Before Yu-cun had finished reading, the sound announcing a visitor was heard, and someone reported, ‘Mr Wang has come to call.’ Yu-cun hurriedly put on his formal robes and cap and went out to receive him. Not until the time it took to eat a meal had passed did he return to ask further questions.

‘These four families are all linked by marriage,’ the usher explained. ‘Harm one and you harm them all; when one prospers, they all prosper. They support one another, cover up for one another, and see that everything is looked after. The Xue accused of this killing is the “snow” in that line about the year of plenty. Nor does his family depend only on the other three. They have plenty of old family friends and relatives of their own, both in the capital and elsewhere. Whom is Your Honour going to arrest now?’
Hearing this, Yu-cun smiled and asked, ‘If that is so, how are we to settle the case?
‘I suppose you also know very well where the murderer is hiding?’

The usher smiled. ‘To tell Your Honour the truth, I know more than where the murderer is. I know the kidnapper too, and I knew the dead buyer very well indeed. Let me tell you the whole story. The fellow who was killed was a local minor landowner’s son called Feng Yuan. Both his parents died when he was a child, and he had no brothers. He lived alone on the little property they had left him. By the time he was eighteen or nineteen he was passionately fond of men and detested women. It must have been some unhappy debt from a former life: he happened to see this kidnapper offering the girl for sale and took a fancy to her at first sight. He made up his mind to buy her as a concubine and swore he would have no more dealings with men,

‘nor take another woman after her. That was why she was to enter his household three days later. Who could have known the kidnapper would secretly sell her again to the Xues? He meant to pocket both families’ money and escape to another province. But he failed to get away. Both families caught him and beat him within an inch of his life. Neither would take its money back; each insisted on having the girl. Young Master Xue was hardly one to yield. He shouted to his men to lay into them, and they beat young Feng to a pulp. Feng was carried home and died three days later. Now, this young Master Xue had already fixed the day for going up to the capital. He happened to come upon the girl two days before he was due to leave, and meant to buy her and take her with him. Then all this trouble broke out.

‘Once he had had Feng beaten and seized the girl, he simply took his family and went on his way as though nothing had happened. There were kinsmen and servants here to deal with the matter. It was not as if a little business like this were worth his running away from.
‘But leave that aside. Who do you suppose the girl being sold was, sir?’
‘How should I know?’ Yu-cun said with a smile.
The usher gave a cold laugh. ‘In a manner of speaking, sir, she is one of your great benefactors. She is the daughter of Mr Zhen, who lived beside the Gourd Temple. Her name is Ying-lian.’
Yu-cun was astonished. ‘So it was she! I heard that she was kidnapped when she was five. Has she only now been put up for sale?’

‘That sort of kidnapper specialises in stealing children of five or six,’ said the usher. ‘He keeps them somewhere out of the way until they are eleven or twelve, then takes them to another district and sells them according to their looks. We used to play with Ying-lian and amuse her every day. Seven or eight years have passed, and she must be twelve or thirteen now. She has grown much prettier, but her features are still much the same. Anyone who knew her would recognise her easily. Besides, she had a red birthmark the size of a grain of rice between her eyebrows. She was born with it. That was how I recognised her.

‘As it happened, the kidnapper had rented some rooms of mine. One day when he was out, I questioned her. But he had beaten her till she was terrified of him, and she dared not tell me a thing. She would only say that he was her own father, and was selling her because he had no money to pay his debts. I tried coaxing her again and again. Then she cried and said only, “I cannot remember when I was little!” That left me in no doubt.

‘The day young Feng came to look at her and paid over the silver, the kidnapper got drunk. She sighed to herself, “At last I must have paid for all my sins!” But when she heard that Feng had ordered her to be brought home three days later, she grew troubled again.

‘I could not bear to see her like that. When the kidnapper went out, I sent my wife to comfort her. “Young Master Feng insists on waiting for a lucky day to fetch you,” she told her. “That shows he does not mean to treat you as a maid. Besides, he is a very handsome, charming young man, and comfortably off. He has always hated women; yet now he is paying such a price for you. You can imagine what that means for your future. You have only two or three days to wait. Why be so unhappy?” That eased her mind a little, and she thought she had found a home at last.

‘Who could have dreamed things would turn out so badly? The very next day the man sold her again, to the Xues. It might have been all right if he had sold her to anyone else. But this young Master Xue, the one they call the “Stupid Tyrant”, is the most wilful, overbearing creature in the world, and spends money like dirt. So he had them thrashed to pieces and Ying-lian was dragged away by force. I do not even know whether she is alive or dead. Poor Feng had all that happiness for nothing. Before he could realise a single hope, he had lost both his money and his life. Is it not pitiful?’
Yu-cun sighed too. ‘Their burden of past sins had brought them to this unhappy pass. There was nothing accidental about it.

‘Otherwise, why should Feng Yuan have set his heart on Ying-lian of all people? After all those years of torment at the kidnapper’s hands, she had at last found a way out, with someone who loved her too. It would have been a happy thing if they could have come together. Instead, this had to happen.

‘The Xues may be richer and grander than the Fengs, but, from the sort of man he is, I imagine he has any number of concubines and indulges himself without restraint. He may be very far from Feng Yuan, who gave his heart to one woman only. A bond of love as fleeting as a dream, and two ill-fated young people brought together! But let us leave them. What I need to know is how best to decide this case.’

The usher smiled. ‘Your Honour used to be so clear-headed and decisive. How is it that you cannot make up your mind today? I hear it was through the Jia and Wang families that you obtained this new appointment. Xue Pan is a relative of the Jias. Why not go with the current, do them a thorough good turn and settle the case? Then you will have something to say when you next call on the Jias and the Wangs.’

‘There is much in what you say,’ Yu-cun replied. ‘But a man’s life is involved. His Majesty’s great kindness in reinstating me and entrusting me with office has given me a second life. This is the very time when I ought to devote every effort to repaying him. How can I set the law aside for private interests? I truly could not bring myself to do it.’
The usher gave a cold laugh. ‘Your Honour’s principles are excellent. Only they will not work in the world as it is today.

‘Have you not heard the old sayings, “A man of mettle acts as the times require”, and “The wise gentleman seeks good fortune and avoids disaster”? If you do as you say, you will not serve the court, and you will not be safe yourself. You had better think it over very carefully.’
Yu-cun kept his head lowered for a long time. At last he spoke.
‘What would you do?’

‘I have already thought of an excellent plan,’ the usher said. ‘When Your Honour takes your seat in court tomorrow, make a great show of authority. Issue documents and warrants for arrests. Naturally, the actual killer will not be found. The complainant is bound to insist that some of the Xue clansmen and servants be arrested and questioned under torture. I shall arrange things behind the scenes and have them report that Xue Pan has died of a sudden illness. His clansmen and the local people can jointly submit a written guarantee of the fact. Your Honour need only claim to be skilled at spirit-writing and summoning immortals. Have an altar set up in court, and invite soldiers and civilians alike to watch. Then announce: “The immortal has given his verdict through the writing-planchette. Feng Yuan and Xue Pan were brought together by a debt from a former life. Having met on a narrow path with no room to pass, they were bound to settle it. Xue Pan has now succumbed to a nameless illness. Pursued by Feng’s ghost, he has died. All the trouble was caused by a certain kidnapper, a man of such-and-such a name from such-and-such a place. He is to be dealt with according to law; no one else need be implicated.” Something of that sort. I shall privately instruct the kidnapper to make a confession agreeing with it.

‘Once people see that the immortal’s pronouncement agrees with the kidnapper’s confession, they will naturally believe the rest of it too. The Xues have money enough. Your Honour may order them to pay a thousand taels, or five hundred, towards the Feng family’s funeral expenses. There is no one of any consequence among the Fengs. All they want is money, and once they get it, I imagine they will have nothing more to say. What does Your Honour think of the plan?’
‘No, that will not do,’ Yu-cun said with a smile. ‘Let me think it over again. Perhaps there is a way to silence the talk.’

It was already late by the time they had finished their discussion, and there is nothing more to tell of that evening. The next day Yu-cun took his seat in court and summoned all those named in the case. He examined them closely and found that, as he had been told, there were few people left in the Feng household, and they were merely using the case to obtain a larger sum for funeral expenses.

The Xues, relying on their power and connections, had refused to yield, which was why the affair had been turned this way and that without a settlement. Yu-cun now bent the law to favour his patrons and disposed of the case in a muddle. The Fengs received a substantial sum for funeral expenses and had little more to say. As soon as he had decided the case, Yu-cun hurriedly wrote two letters, one to Jia Zheng and the other to Wang Zi-teng, Commander of the Metropolitan Garrison. They said little more than, ‘Your nephew’s affair has been settled. There is no need for further concern.’

The whole arrangement had originated with the former novice of the Gourd Temple, now an usher. Yu-cun, however, feared that he might tell people about his earlier days of poverty and low estate, and was deeply uneasy. In the end he found some fault with the man and had him sent far away into penal exile. Only then was he satisfied.

But we need say no more of Yu-cun for the present. Let us return to the young Master Xue who had bought Ying-lian and had Feng Yuan beaten to death. He too was a native of Jinling, born into a family with a tradition of scholarship. He had lost his father as a child, however, and his widowed mother, cherishing him as her only son, had spoilt and indulged him until he grew up good for nothing. The family possessed a fortune reckoned in millions, and currently received funds from the imperial privy treasury to purchase miscellaneous supplies.

The young man’s formal name was Xue Pan, and his courtesy name Wen-long. Even at five he had been extravagant in his tastes and arrogant in his speech. He had attended school, but knew little more than a few characters, and spent his days at cockfights and horse races, or roaming the hills and enjoying the scenery. Though an imperial purveyor, he knew nothing at all of business or practical affairs. Old ties with his grandfather and father kept his name nominally on the Board of Revenue’s books and allowed him to draw the allotted funds. Everything else was attended to by the clerks and the old family servants.

His widowed mother, née Wang, was a younger sister of Wang Zi-teng, the present Commander of the Metropolitan Garrison, and a sister by the same mother of Lady Wang, Jia Zheng’s wife at the Rong mansion. She was only about forty, and Xue Pan was her only son. She also had a daughter, two years younger than Xue Pan, whose childhood name was Bao-chai. The girl’s skin had a smooth, lustrous bloom, and her manner was composed and graceful. Her father had adored her and had her taught to read, and she was ten times the scholar her brother was. After her father’s death, seeing that her brother could do little to comfort their mother, she gave up making books her chief concern and turned instead to needlework and household affairs, hoping to ease her mother’s worries and spare her some labour.

Now the present sovereign, who honoured poetry and ritual and sought out talent, had recently bestowed an extraordinary favour. In addition to the selection of imperial consorts, the names of daughters from distinguished official families were all to be submitted to the appropriate board, so that some might be chosen as study companions for princesses of the imperial and princely houses, with appointments as Ladies of Talent and Ladies of Instruction. There was another consideration too. Since Xue Pan’s father had died, the managers and clerks of the family’s businesses and supply agencies in the provinces, seeing how young and inexperienced Xue Pan was, had seized the opportunity to cheat him. Several of the businesses in the capital were dwindling away as well.

Xue Pan had long heard that the capital was the most splendid and prosperous place in the world, and had been thinking of going there. He took this opportunity to do so: first, to escort his sister there for the selection; second, to visit relatives; and third, to settle the old accounts in person at the Board and arrange for new advances. His real purpose was to see the sights of the imperial city.

He had accordingly packed his baggage and valuables well beforehand, together with local specialities and other gifts for relatives and friends. Just as an auspicious day had been chosen and his departure fixed, he happened to encounter the kidnapper selling Ying-lian a second time. Struck by her unusual beauty, he was determined to buy her. When the Fengs came to claim her, he relied on his superior strength and ordered his brutal servants to beat Feng Yuan to death. Then, having entrusted every detail of the household’s affairs to his clansmen and a few old servants, he set off on his long journey with his mother and sister. To him a homicide case was child’s play. He thought there was nothing that a little filthy money would not settle.

We need not count the days they spent on the road. As they were nearing the capital, they heard that his maternal uncle Wang Zi-teng had been promoted to Commander-in-Chief of Nine Provinces and ordered to leave the capital on an inspection of the frontiers.
Xue Pan was secretly delighted.

‘I was just worrying that my own mother’s brother would be there to keep me in order,’ he thought, ‘and I would not be free to spend and enjoy myself as I pleased. Now he has been promoted and sent away! Heaven does give a man what he wants.’
He broached the matter with his mother.

‘We have several houses in the capital, but none of us has lived there for ten years or more. The caretakers are sure to have been letting them out on the quiet. We ought to send a few men ahead to clean up and put things in order.’

‘Why make such a fuss?’ his mother said. ‘The first thing we ought to do on reaching the capital is visit our relatives and friends. We can stay either with your uncle or with your aunt’s husband. Both houses have very convenient accommodation. Why not settle in at one of them first, and then have our own house put in order at leisure? It would be much less trouble.’

‘But my uncle has just been promoted to a post outside the capital. His household will be busy getting ready to leave. Surely it would be rather tactless for the whole lot of us to descend on them just now.’

‘Even if your uncle is moving away, there is still your aunt’s husband,’ his mother replied. ‘And for years now both your uncle’s and your aunt’s households have been sending letters and messages inviting us to come. Now that we are here, your uncle may be busy leaving, but your aunt at the Jias’ is sure to press us to stay. If we rush about getting our own house ready, will people not take offence? I know what you are thinking. Living with your uncle or your aunt’s husband would put a check on you. You would rather live on your own and do just as you please. Very well, then. Go and choose a house for yourself. Your aunt and I have not seen each other for years, and I want to spend a few days with her. I shall take your sister and stay at her house. How does that suit you?’
Xue Pan knew from this that he could not get his way. He had to tell the men to take them straight to the Rong mansion.

Lady Wang had already heard how Jia Yu-cun had intervened to settle Xue Pan’s case, and her mind was now at ease. Then came the news of her brother’s promotion to a frontier post. She was feeling rather lonely at the thought that there would be one fewer member of her own family to see. A few days later a servant suddenly announced, ‘Your sister has brought the young master and young lady to the capital. The whole family is outside, getting out of the carriages.’

Delighted, Lady Wang hurried out to the main hall with the girls and daughters-in-law to welcome Aunt Xue and bring them in. The sisters were meeting again in their later years: there is no need to describe their mingled grief and joy, their tears and laughter as they spoke of their long separation. Lady Wang hastened to take them to pay their respects to Grandmother Jia, and the various presents and local specialities were offered. When everyone in the household had greeted them, a welcoming feast was quickly prepared.
Xue Pan had already paid his respects to Jia Zheng, and Jia Lian took him to see Jia She, Jia Zhen and the others. Jia Zheng sent a message in to Lady Wang:

‘Your sister is getting on in years, and our nephew is young and knows nothing of the world. If they live outside, I fear someone may make trouble for them. There are a dozen rooms standing empty in Pear-tree Court, in the north-east corner of our grounds. It would be an excellent arrangement to have them cleaned and invite your sister and the two young people to stay there.’
Before Lady Wang could urge them to stay, Grandmother Jia too sent to say, ‘Ask your sister to make her home here, so that we can all be closer.’

Aunt Xue had wanted just such an arrangement, which would allow her to keep a tighter hold on her son. If they lived separately, she feared he would give his temper free rein and get into trouble again. She therefore thanked them warmly and accepted. In private, however, she made one point clear to Lady Wang:
‘You must leave all our daily expenses and provisions to us. That is the only way we can go on comfortably together.’
Lady Wang knew that her sister’s family could well afford them, and agreed. From then on Aunt Xue and her children lived in Pear-tree Court.

Pear-tree Court had been the old Duke of Rong’s retreat in his later years. It was a neat little place of a dozen rooms or so, complete with a hall at the front and living quarters behind. A separate gate opened on to the street, and the Xue servants used it to come and go. In the south-west corner a side gate led into a narrow passage, which emerged on the east side of Lady Wang’s principal rooms. Every day, either after a meal or in the evening, Aunt Xue would come over to chat with Grandmother Jia or spend time with Lady Wang. Bao-chai passed her days with Dai-yu, Ying-chun and the other girls, reading, playing chess or doing needlework, and was very happy.

Xue Pan had originally been unwilling to live in the Jia household, fearing that his uncle would keep him in order and give him no freedom. But his mother was determined to stay, and the family pressed them so warmly that he had to remain for the time being. Meanwhile, he sent men to prepare one of his own houses, intending to move there later. Yet before he had been there a month he had become well acquainted with half the sons and nephews of the Jia clan. Every one of its idle young rakes was delighted to make his acquaintance. There was a drinking party today, an outing to see the flowers tomorrow; then came gambling parties and visits to prostitutes, until by degrees there was nothing they would not do. Under their influence Xue Pan grew ten times worse than before.

Jia Zheng had sound methods of bringing up his sons and firm rules for his household. But in the first place, the clan was too large, with too many members, for him to supervise all this. In the second, its present head was Jia Zhen, the eldest grandson of the Ning branch, who had also inherited its rank. Clan affairs were his responsibility. Thirdly, Jia Zheng had more than enough public and private business to attend to, and was by nature a man of easy detachment who set little store by mundane affairs. In his hours away from official work he merely read or played chess, paying little attention to anything else. Moreover, Pear-tree Court was two ranges of buildings away and had its own street gate, through which anyone could come and go at will. The young men were therefore quite free to enjoy themselves as they pleased, and Xue Pan gradually abandoned all thought of moving out.
We have briefly related how the Xue family, mother and children, came to stay at the Rong mansion, and must leave them for the present. Let us turn instead to Lin Dai-yu.

Ever since her arrival at the Rong mansion, Grandmother Jia had lavished affection on her. In everything, from meals and sleeping arrangements to the ordering of her day, she was treated just like Bao-yu; the old lady’s own three granddaughters, Ying-chun, Tan-chun and Xi-chun, had to take second place. The closeness and affection between Bao-yu and Dai-yu were quite unlike their relations with anyone else. By day they went about together and sat together; at night they rested in the same quarters. In word and thought they were in perfect accord, with scarcely a moment’s estrangement. But now Xue Bao-chai had suddenly appeared. Although only a little older, she had a composed, upright manner and a full, lovely face, and many thought Dai-yu no match for her. Bao-chai was easygoing, accommodating herself to people and circumstances, unlike Dai-yu, who held herself proudly apart and disdained anything she thought beneath her. Consequently she was far more popular with the servants. Even the little maids generally preferred to go and play with Bao-chai. This left Dai-yu feeling somewhat depressed and resentful, though Bao-chai was entirely unaware of it. Bao-yu was still a child. Moreover, with the simple-minded, contrary nature he had been born with, he felt the same towards all his brothers, sisters and cousins, making no distinction between close relations and distant ones.

Because he and Dai-yu shared Grandmother Jia’s quarters, he was a little more familiar with her than with the other girls. Familiarity brought greater intimacy; intimacy, in turn, inevitably brought the occasional reproach for falling short of perfection, the unexpected breach. On this particular day, for some reason or other, the two had disagreed. Dai-yu was once more crying alone in her room, while Bao-yu,

regretting his own rash words, went to make peace with her. Only then did she gradually relent. The plum blossom was now at its height in the garden of the Ning mansion to the east, and Jia Zhen’s wife, You-shi, arranged a party for Grandmother Jia, Lady Xing, Lady Wang and the others to enjoy it. That day she brought Jia Rong’s wife with her to deliver the invitation in person. Grandmother Jia and her party went over after breakfast and amused themselves in the Garden of Gathered Fragrance, taking tea first and wine afterwards. It was merely a small family gathering of the women from the Ning and Rong households; there were no other novelties or amusing incidents to record. Presently Bao-yu grew tired and wanted his midday nap. Grandmother Jia told his attendants to coax him gently to sleep and bring him back when he had rested. Jia Rong’s wife, Qin-shi, promptly answered with a smile, ‘We have a room all ready for Uncle Bao. Don’t worry, Great-grandmother. Just leave him to me.’ Then she turned to his nurse and maids. ‘Mamma, sisters, please bring Uncle Bao this way with me.’ Grandmother Jia had always known Qin-shi to be thoroughly capable. Delicate and graceful in appearance, gentle and even-tempered in her dealings, she was the old lady’s favourite among her great-grandsons’ wives. With Qin-shi seeing to Bao-yu, she naturally felt quite at ease.

Qin-shi led the whole party to an inner room in the main apartments. Bao-yu looked up and saw a picture mounted on the wall. The figures were beautifully painted, but its subject was The Burning Goosefoot Staff, and without even looking to see who the painter was, he began to feel displeased. Beside it hung a pair of scrolls: ‘A thorough knowledge of worldly affairs is learning; / A practised understanding of human dealings is literature.’ Once he had read those two lines, he would not stay, however exquisite the room and sumptuous its furnishings. ‘Let’s go out! Quickly!’ he cried. ‘If this won’t do, where can we go?’ Qin-shi said, laughing. ‘Unless you come to my room.’ Bao-yu nodded and smiled. ‘Who ever heard of an uncle sleeping in his nephew’s room?’ one of the old women objected. ‘Oh, dear me!’ Qin-shi laughed. ‘I hope he won’t be offended, but how old is he, that we should already worry about such things? Didn’t you see my brother when he came last month? He’s the same age as Uncle Bao, but put them side by side, and I rather think my brother would be the taller.’ ‘How is it I’ve never seen him?’ Bao-yu asked.

‘Bring him here for me to see.’ Everyone laughed. ‘With twenty or thirty li between us? How are we to fetch him here? You’ll have plenty of chances to meet.’ As they spoke, they reached Qin-shi’s room. At the doorway a faint, sweet fragrance came wafting towards them. Bao-yu’s eyes grew heavy, his limbs relaxed, and he kept saying, ‘What a lovely scent!’
Inside, he looked at the wall and saw Tang Bo-hu’s painting Spring Sleep among the Crab-apple Blossoms. On either side hung a couplet written by the Song scholar Qin Tai-xu:
A gentle chill confines the dream: spring is still cold;
Fragrance enfolds the sleeper: wine perfumes the air.

On the table stood the precious mirror that had once furnished Wu Ze-tian’s mirror chamber. To one side was the golden platter on which Flying Swallow had danced; in it lay the quince An Lu-shan had thrown, bruising Tai-zhen’s breast. Further in stood the couch on which Princess Shou-chang had slept below the Hanzhang Hall, hung with the strung-pearl curtains Princess Tong-chang had had made. ‘This is lovely!’ Bao-yu said again and again, smiling. ‘I dare say even an immortal could live in this room of mine,’ Qin-shi said with a laugh. With her own hands she spread a gauze coverlet washed by Xi Shi and moved into place a lovers’ pillow once held by Hong-niang. The nurses settled Bao-yu in bed and gradually withdrew, leaving only the four maids Aroma, Winsome, Skybright and Musk to keep him company. Qin-shi told the little maids to keep a good watch under the eaves in case the cats and dogs started fighting.

Bao-yu had scarcely closed his eyes before he drifted off to sleep. It still seemed that Qin-shi was before him, and he floated along behind her until they reached a place of red balustrades, white stone, green trees and clear streams, where human footsteps seldom came and no dust could reach. Delighted in his dream, he thought, ‘What an interesting place! I’d willingly spend my whole life here, even if it meant losing my home. It would be better than being beaten by my parents and teachers every day.’ While these idle thoughts were passing through his head, he suddenly heard someone singing beyond the hill:
Spring dreams disperse with the clouds;
Fallen flowers follow the flowing stream.
A word to all you girls and boys:
Why go in search of needless sorrow?

Bao-yu could tell that it was a woman’s voice. Before the song had ended, a figure emerged, moving with a light, slender grace quite unlike that of ordinary mortals. A descriptive verse bears witness:

She leaves the willow hollow, steps from her flowery bower.
Where she walks, birds start in the courtyard trees;
as she approaches, her shadow crosses the winding gallery.
Her immortal sleeves stir: musk and orchid breathe around her;
her lotus robe begins to move: her girdle pendants chime.
Her dimples smile like peach blossom in spring beneath cloud-dark coils of hair;
her lips part, red as cherries, her pomegranate-seed teeth hold fragrance.
Her slender waist turns like snow dancing in a circling wind;
pearls and kingfisher jewels gleam above a brow adorned with yellow.
Among the flowers, now hidden, now seen, she is lovely in anger or joy;
beside the pool she lingers, seeming to rise and fly.
Her moth-fine brows smile and frown; she is about to speak, but has not spoken.
Her lotus steps begin: she would pause, yet means to go.
Admire the beauty of her being: clear as ice, lustrous as jade;
admire her splendid robes, their patterns flashing bright.
Love her face, as though nurtured on fragrance and carved of jade;
praise her bearing, a phoenix soaring, a dragon in flight.
Her unadorned fairness? Spring plum blossom opening in snow.
Her purity? An autumn chrysanthemum mantled in frost.
Her stillness? A pine growing in an empty valley.
Her splendour? Rosy clouds reflected in a clear pool.
Her elegance? A dragon moving through a winding lake.
Her spirit? Moonlight striking a cold river.
Xi Shi must feel ashamed beside her, Wang Qiang abashed.
How wondrous! Where was she born, from what country does she come?
Indeed, the Jasper Pool has no second such beauty, the Purple Palace no equal.
Who can she be, so lovely as this?

Seeing that she was an immortal, Bao-yu hurried forward in delight and bowed with clasped hands. ‘Immortal sister, where have you come from, and where are you going? I don’t even know what this place is. Please, would you take me with you?’

The immortal smiled. ‘I dwell above the Heaven of Parting Sorrow, amid the Sea of Grief. I am Fairy Disenchantment, of the Land of Illusion, in the Cave of Dispersed Fragrance on Mount of Released Spring. I oversee the debts of love and desire among mortals, and govern women’s resentments and men’s infatuations in the dusty world. Lately certain tangled debts of passion have become bound up with this place, so I have come to examine the opportunities and spread the longing of lovers. Our meeting today is no accident either. My domain is not far away. I have little to offer: just a cup of immortal tea I picked myself, a jar of fine wine of my own brewing, a few singing girls practised in enchanted dances, and twelve newly written immortal songs called Dream of the Red Chamber. Will you come and visit it with me?’ Hearing this, Bao-yu forgot all about where Qin-shi might be and followed the fairy. They reached a stone archway bearing the great inscription ‘LAND OF ILLUSION’. On either side was a couplet:
When the false is taken as true, the true is also false;
Where nothing passes for something, something returns to nothing.
Beyond the archway stood a palace gate, bearing the inscription ‘SEA OF KARMIC DEBT, HEAVEN OF PASSION’.
Another couplet was written there in large characters:
Deep earth, high heaven: alas, love never ends, in any age;
Besotted men, resentful women: how hard to pay the debts of love!

‘So that’s how it is,’ Bao-yu thought after reading it. ‘But what is this love through all the ages? What are these debts of love? From now on I must find out about them.’ He merely thought it to himself, little knowing that he had already invited evil influences into the deepest recesses of his being. Following the fairy through a second gateway, he came to the side halls. All had plaques and couplets, too many to read at once. He noticed only a few: ‘Office of Infatuation’, ‘Office of Accumulated Resentment’, ‘Office of Morning Tears’, ‘Office of Night-time Grievances’, ‘Office of Spring Longings’ and ‘Office of Autumn Sorrow’. Having read them, he asked the fairy, ‘Could I trouble you to show me round these different offices? Would that be allowed?’ ‘These offices hold the records of the past and future of every woman under heaven,’ she said. ‘With your mortal eyes and earthly body, you cannot be permitted to know them beforehand.’ Bao-yu would not take no for an answer, and begged her again and again.
At last the fairy had to yield. ‘Very well. You may pay a brief visit to this one office.’ Overjoyed, Bao-yu looked up at its plaque: ‘OFFICE OF THE ILL-FATED’. The couplet on either side read:
Spring’s regrets and autumn’s sorrows are all of your own making;
For whom do flowerlike faces, moonlike beauties bloom?

Reading this, Bao-yu felt moved to sigh. Inside he saw a dozen or more large cupboards, all sealed with strips of paper bearing the names of the various provinces. He was so intent on finding the label for his own native place that he paid no attention to the others.

On a cupboard over to one side he saw a seal marked in large characters ‘MAIN REGISTER OF THE TWELVE BEAUTIES OF JINLING’. ‘What does “Main Register of the Twelve Beauties of Jinling” mean?’ he asked. ‘It records the twelve foremost women of your province,’ Disenchantment replied. ‘That is why it is called the Main Register.’ ‘People always say Jinling is enormous,’ said Bao-yu. ‘How can it have only twelve women? In our household alone, counting high and low, there are several hundred girls.’ Disenchantment gave a cold laugh. ‘There are indeed many women in your province. We have selected only those of consequence to enter here. Those in the two cupboards below rank next. As for the ordinary run of women, there are no registers for them.’ Looking at the two lower cupboards, Bao-yu saw that one was indeed labelled ‘SUPPLEMENTARY REGISTER OF THE TWELVE BEAUTIES OF JINLING’, and the other ‘SECOND SUPPLEMENTARY REGISTER OF THE TWELVE BEAUTIES OF JINLING’.

He first reached out to open the cupboard of the Second Supplementary Register. He took out a volume and opened it. On the first page was a picture, neither of people nor of a landscape: nothing but black clouds and murky mist washed across the paper in watery ink. A few lines were written there:
A moon after rain is seldom seen; bright clouds soon scatter.
Her heart stands higher than the sky; her station is lowly.
Her charm and cleverness provoke resentment.
Slander, more than anything, cuts short her years;
The loving young master grieves for her in vain.
Turning the page, Bao-yu saw a cluster of fresh flowers and a torn sleeping mat. Here too were a few lines:
Gentleness and obedience, all in vain;
In vain they call her cassia-sweet and orchid-fair.
Alas, an actor is the fortunate one;
Who knew the young master’s bond with her would fail?

Bao-yu could make nothing of it. Tossing the volume aside, he opened the cupboard of the Supplementary Register and took out another. In it he saw a flowering cassia tree, with a pool below: its water gone, its mud dried out, the lotus withered and its roots decayed. Behind the picture was written:
Her root beside the lotus, a single fragrant stem;
The fortunes of her life are sad indeed.
Once a lone tree springs from two patches of earth,
Her fragrant soul is sent back to its native home.

Bao-yu still did not understand. He tossed this volume aside too, and took out the Main Register. The first page showed two dead trees with a jade belt hanging from their branches, and a heap of snow with a golden hairpin beneath it. Four lines accompanied the picture:
Alas for the virtue that stopped the loom;
Alas for the wit that sang of willow fluff!
A jade belt hangs among the trees;
A golden hairpin lies buried in snow.

Again Bao-yu could make nothing of it. He wanted to ask, but knew she would never reveal the secret; he wanted to put the book down, but could not bear to. Turning on, he saw a bow with a citron hanging from it. A verse was written there:
For twenty years she has discerned the right from wrong;
Where pomegranate flowers open, light fills the palace chambers.
How can the three springs rival the first spring’s splendour?
Tiger and wild buffalo meet; she returns from the great dream.
The next picture showed two people flying kites, a great expanse of sea and a large ship. In the ship was a woman covering her face and weeping. There were four lines:
Her mind is keen, her aspirations high;
Born in a failing age, her fortune wanes.
At Clear Brightness, tears of parting, eyes turned towards the river;
A thousand li of east wind: even a dream is far away.
Next came a few wisps of flying cloud and a stretch of flowing water. The words ran:
What use are rank and wealth? In swaddling clothes she loses both her parents.
In a blink she mourns the setting sun: the Xiang’s waters pass, the clouds of Chu fly on.
The next picture showed a beautiful piece of jade fallen in the dirt. Its verdict read:
She longs to be pure, but when was she pure? She speaks of emptiness, yet may not be empty.
Alas for a nature of gold and jade, sunk at last in mire!
Next, suddenly, came a vicious wolf pursuing and leaping at a beautiful woman, as if to devour her. The writing read:
Child joined to thread: a wolf of Zhongshan;
Once you get your way, you run wild.
A flower-and-willow beauty from a noble chamber,
Within a year she enters the millet dream.
Next was an ancient temple, with a beautiful woman sitting alone inside, reading a sutra. The verdict ran:
Seeing through the three springs’ brief splendour,
She suddenly exchanges her old finery for a dark religious robe.
Alas, a marquis’s daughter from embroidered chambers,
Now sleeps alone beside a dim lamp and an ancient Buddha.
Next came an iceberg with a female phoenix on it. Its verdict read:
An ordinary bird comes, of all times, in the last days;
All know and admire her gifts.
First obedience, then command, then person and tree;
Weeping towards Jinling, her story grows more grievous still.
Next was a deserted village and a lonely wayside inn, with a beautiful woman spinning there. The verdict read:
When power fails, speak no more of rank;
When the family falls, count no more on kin.
Because she once chanced to help a woman named Liu,
By a lucky chance she meets a benefactor.
The next picture showed a pot of flourishing orchids. Beside it stood a beautiful woman wearing a phoenix coronet and a ceremonial cape. It too had a verdict:
Peach and plum in spring winds bear their finished fruit;
In the end, who can match that pot of orchids?
Goodness like ice and water is envied to no purpose;
In vain, it gives the others something to laugh about.
Next was a lofty mansion, with a beautiful woman hanging from a beam. Its verdict read:
Passion’s heaven and sea conjure a body of passion; when passion meets its counterpart, lust must prevail.
Do not say all the unworthy come from Rong: the first provocation to disaster lies in Ning.

Bao-yu wanted to read on, but the fairy knew how bright his natural gifts were, how quick his understanding, and feared that heaven’s secrets might be disclosed. She closed the volume and said with a smile, ‘Come and see the marvels with me. Why stay here puzzling over these riddles?’ In a haze, Bao-yu let the register go without quite knowing it and followed Disenchantment to the rear. There were pearl curtains, embroidered hangings, painted beams and carved eaves: words could not exhaust the light that played on crimson doors and floors of gold, or the snowy brilliance of jasper windows and palaces of jade. Immortal flowers and rare grasses filled the air with fragrance. It was a wonderful place indeed. Disenchantment called out, laughing, ‘Come quickly and welcome our honoured guest!’ Before she had finished, several immortals came out of the rooms, their lotus sleeves fluttering, their feather robes swaying, lovely as spring flowers and alluring as the autumn moon. The moment they saw Bao-yu, they reproached Disenchantment. ‘We wondered what “honoured guest” this could be, and hurried out to meet him! You said that at this very hour today our little sister Crimson Pearl’s living soul would come to visit, and we have been waiting for so long.

‘Why have you brought this filthy creature instead, to pollute our pure realm of girls?’ Hearing them, Bao-yu was so frightened that he wanted to retreat but could not, and truly felt himself unutterably unclean. Disenchantment quickly took his hand and said to her sisters, ‘You do not know the circumstances. Today I meant to go to the Rong mansion to fetch Crimson Pearl, but as I passed the Ning mansion I happened to meet the spirits of the Dukes of Ning and Rong. They charged me with this request: “Since our dynasty was established, our family has enjoyed distinction in generation after generation, passing wealth and honour down for a hundred years. But now our allotted fortune is spent, and nothing can turn it back. Though we have left many descendants, not one can carry on our work. Only Bao-yu, a grandson in the legitimate line, offers some hope. His disposition is perverse, his nature strange and unpredictable, but he is intelligent and quick-witted, and something might be made of him. Unfortunately our family’s term of fortune is due to end, and we fear there will be no one to guide him to the proper path. Since you have chanced to come, fairy, we beg you first to warn his stubborn, infatuated nature through matters of passion and desire, music and beauty. Perhaps he may break out of their beguiling circle and then enter the right way. That would be a blessing to us brothers.” Because they asked this of me, I took pity and brought him here.

‘First I let him study the lifelong records of the women of his household in all three ranks, upper, middle and lower, but still he did not awaken. So I have brought him here to experience further illusions of feasting, music and beauty. Who knows? Perhaps he will one day understand.’ With that, she led Bao-yu indoors. A thread of delicate scent reached him, but he had no idea what was burning, and could not help asking. Disenchantment gave a cold laugh. ‘How could you know it, when no such incense exists in the mortal world? It is made of the essence of rare flowers at their first budding in famous mountains and places of beauty, blended with oils from precious forests and jewelled trees. Its name is Marrow of All Flowers.’

Bao-yu could only admire it. They all sat down, and little maids brought tea. He found its fresh fragrance and unfamiliar flavour extraordinarily pure and delicious, and asked its name as well. ‘This tea comes from the Cave of Dispersed Fragrance on Mount of Released Spring,’ said Disenchantment. ‘It is brewed with dew that has lain overnight on immortal flowers and numinous leaves. Its name is A Thousand Reds in One Cavern.’ Bao-yu nodded appreciatively. Looking round the room, he saw that nothing was lacking: a precious qin, fine incense tripods, old paintings and new poems. He was still more pleased to find bits of embroidery floss spat out beneath the window and occasional powder stains among the dressing boxes. A couplet hung on the wall:
A place of subtle mystery and spiritual grace;
A heaven where nothing can be done.

Bao-yu admired everything he read. He then asked the names of the immortals. One was the Fairy of Infatuated Dreams, another the Great Being of Devoted Love, another the Golden Maiden Who Draws Sorrow, and another the Bodhi of Passage beyond Grief. Each had a different religious name. Presently little maids came to arrange tables and chairs and lay out food and wine. Truly, precious nectar brimmed in glass goblets; rich jade liquor filled the amber cups.

There is no need to dwell on the abundance of the dishes. Finding the wine unusually fragrant, sweet and clear, Bao-yu could not resist asking about it too. ‘This wine is brewed from the stamens of a hundred flowers and the sap of ten thousand trees,’ Disenchantment told him, ‘with a ferment of qilin marrow and a starter of phoenix milk. That is why it is called Ten Thousand Beauties in One Cup.’ Bao-yu could not praise it enough.

As they drank, twelve dancing girls came forward and asked which songs they should perform. ‘Give us the twelve newly composed songs of Dream of the Red Chamber,’ said Disenchantment. The girls assented, tapped their sandalwood clappers softly and gently played their silver-strung zithers.

They began to sing, ‘When primal chaos first broke open…’ They had sung only that one phrase when Disenchantment said, ‘These songs are not like the dramatic songs written in the mortal world, which must observe the conventions of male lead, female lead, painted face and supporting male roles, and the restrictions of the nine musical modes of north and south. Here one song may lament a person, another reflect on an event. A song comes to us, and we can set it straight to pipes and strings. Unless you have experienced these things yourself,

‘you cannot know their beauty. I doubt that you will fully understand these songs either. Unless you read the text before listening to the singing, it will be like chewing wax.’ She turned and told a little maid to fetch the original manuscript of Dream of the Red Chamber and hand it to Bao-yu. He took it, reading the words as he listened to the song:
[Dream of the Red Chamber: Prelude]

Since primal chaos first broke open,
who was born a creature of love?
It all springs from love’s passion for the moon and wind.
In this helpless heaven,
on this sorrowing day,
in this lonely hour,
let me try to give voice to my foolish heart.
And so we perform this Dream of the Red Chamber,
cherishing gold, mourning jade.
[A Life Mismatched]

They all proclaim the happy match of gold and jade;
I think only of the former pledge of wood and stone.
In vain I face the mountain recluse’s glittering snow;
I cannot forget the lonely forest of that fairy beyond the world.
Alas, only now do I believe
that human happiness is never whole.
Even were the tray raised level with the brows,
still my heart would find no peace.
[Brows Knit in Vain]

One is a flower of the immortal garden,
one a flawless piece of precious jade.
If no strange destiny unites them,
why have they met in this life?
If a strange destiny unites them,
why must their heart’s desire dissolve at last?
One sighs to no purpose;
one wastes all care in vain.
One is the moon in water,
one a flower in a mirror.
