How many tears can there be in those eyes,
to endure the flow from autumn to winter’s end,
from spring into summer?

Bao-yu found the song rambling and groundless, and could see no merit in it. Yet its plaintive melody could quite dissolve his soul and intoxicate his spirit. So he neither examined its meaning nor asked where it came from, but simply let it ease his boredom for the moment. Then he read on:
[Resentment at Impermanence]

Joy in splendour just at its height;
resentment that impermanence has come again.
With open eyes, all things must be abandoned;
drifting, drifting, the fragrant soul is spent.
I look towards home: the road is long, the mountains high.
So I seek my parents in their dreams to tell them:
‘Your child’s life has entered the Yellow Springs.
My dear ones, step back and get free while there is time!’
‘I am going. Do not let me hold you bound.’
[Sorrow within Joy]

In swaddling clothes, alas, both parents lost.
Even dwelling amid fine silks,
who knows the care that cherishes a child?
Fortunately, she was born open-hearted, bold and generous;
never did the private feelings of lovers entangle her heart.
She was like a moon after rain and a clear fresh wind,
shining through a hall of jade.
Matched with a handsome, gifted husband, fair as an immortal,
she won a union that would last as long as heaven and earth,
surely enough to make amends for childhood’s hardships.
Yet in the end the clouds disperse from Gaotang,
the Xiang River’s waters run dry.
Such are the destined ebb and flow of this dusty world.
Why grieve to no purpose?
[No Place in the World]

Her nature lovely as an orchid,
her abundant gifts an immortal’s equal;
born solitary, unlike anyone else.
You call the eating of meat and fish rank,
and find silk finery vulgar and repellent.
Yet you do not know: the loftier you stand, the more they envy;
the purer you are, the more the world dislikes you.
Alas, she will grow old by a dim lamp in an ancient hall,
wasting the fading spring of a painted face in crimson chambers.
In the end there is still the grime of the dusty world,
against her heart’s desire.
As though flawless white jade were sunk in mud.
Why then should princes and young gentlemen
lament that no destined bond was theirs?
[A Welcome Enemy]

Wolf of Zhongshan, heartless beast,
forgetting entirely how it all began!
Nothing but arrogance, extravagance, lust and greed, and further scheming.
He regards that noble beauty as a common willow,
degrades a duke’s daughter as though she were the lowest of the low.
Alas for her lovely, fragrant soul,
drifting away within a year.
[Awakening from Empty Flowers]

See through the three springs:
what then can red peach blossom and green willow do?
Extinguish the splendour of youth;
seek a heart free of passion, at peace with heaven.
What talk of peach trees blooming high in heaven,
of countless apricot stamens among the clouds!
In the end, who endures beyond autumn?
Look: among the white poplars, people sob;
beneath the green maples, ghosts chant.
And withered grass, stretching to the sky,
hides the graves.
Truly, poor yesterday, rich today, people toil;
flowers flourish in spring and fade in autumn, worn away.
Who can escape life’s barriers and death’s ordeals?
They say a precious tree in the West is called the Sala,
and on it grows the fruit of everlasting life.
[Undone by Cleverness]

Every device calculated, clever beyond measure,
she calculates away her own dear life.
Before death her heart is broken;
after death her spirit is empty and free.
A wealthy house, its people at peace:
still there comes the family’s ruin,
its members scattering, each to flee alone.
All for nothing, half a lifetime’s anxious heart,
like a dream adrift at the third watch.
A crash, as a great mansion falls;
a gathering darkness, as a lamp burns low.
Ah! All that joy, suddenly grief and bitterness.
Alas for this world: nothing can be settled!
[Blessings Left Behind]

Blessings left behind, blessings left behind:
a benefactor met by chance.
Fortunate in her mother, fortunate in her mother,
who stored up hidden merit!
Let all people take this counsel:
help the distressed, support the poor.
Do not be like my cruel uncle and treacherous elder cousin,
who love silver and forget their own flesh and blood!
Multiplication, division, addition, subtraction:
heaven above keeps the account.
[Late Splendour]

Affection in a mirror,
and worse, distinction in a dream!
How swiftly lovely youth is gone.
Speak no more of embroidered curtains and lovers’ quilts.
Even wearing a pearl coronet
and a phoenix-patterned robe
cannot offset the impermanence of life.
Though they say none should suffer poverty in old age,
there is still a need to store hidden merit for one’s descendants.
Head held high beneath an official’s hat and tassels;
a golden seal hanging bright at the waist;
rank and stipend mounting in imposing splendour:
then darkness, and the road to the Yellow Springs draws near.
Where are the generals and ministers of old?
Only empty names remain for later people to admire.
[The End of Good Things]

Spring ends at the painted beam; fragrant dust falls.
Skilled in love, possessed of a moonlike face:
these become the roots of the family’s ruin.
The ancestral calling falls to pieces, all from Jing;
for the household’s destruction, Ning bears the first blame.
Old karmic wrongs always spring from passion.
[Finale: Birds Return to Their Woods]

When they had finished, they were about to sing the supplementary songs. Seeing how little interest Bao-yu showed, Disenchantment sighed. ‘The foolish child still has not awakened!’ Bao-yu hastily stopped the singers from going on. Feeling dazed and confused, he pleaded drunkenness and asked to lie down. Disenchantment had the remains of the feast removed and took him to a fragrant, embroidered bedchamber, furnished with splendours such as he had never seen.

Still more astonishing, a young woman was already inside. In the rich freshness of her beauty she resembled Bao-chai; in her graceful charm and slender bearing she was like Dai-yu. He had no idea what this meant. Suddenly Disenchantment spoke. ‘In so many wealthy, distinguished households in the mortal world, the moonlit pleasures behind green windows and the misty splendour of embroidered chambers have all been defiled by debauched young wastrels and loose women. More hateful still, how many frivolous libertines through the ages have excused themselves by saying, “I love beauty but am not lustful,” or pleaded, “I have passion, but not lust.” These are all words to dress up wrongdoing and conceal ugliness.

‘To love beauty is already lust; to know passion is greater lust still. The meetings on Mount Wu, the pleasures of cloud and rain, all come from delighting in someone’s beauty and then becoming attached to their affection. What I value in you is that you are the foremost creature of lust in all the world, ancient or modern.’

Bao-yu was so alarmed that he answered hastily, ‘You are mistaken, fairy. My parents are always scolding me for being lazy about my books. How could I dare to incur the name of “lustful” as well? Besides, I’m still young. I don’t know what “lust” is.’ ‘No,’ said Disenchantment. ‘Though lust has one underlying principle, its meanings differ. Those who delight in lust in the ordinary world merely enjoy good looks, singing and dancing, endless flirting, lovemaking at every hour. They wish all the beauties in the world could serve their momentary pleasure. Such creatures are fools whose excess goes no deeper than the skin. You, however, were born with a strain of devoted feeling that we call “lust of the imagination”. This can be understood in the heart, but not passed on by mouth; grasped in spirit, but not conveyed in words. You alone now possess this quality. It can make you a good companion in the women’s quarters, but out in the world you will inevitably seem impractical and strange, mocked by every tongue, glared at by every eye. Having met your ancestors, the two Dukes of Ning and Rong, and heard their heartfelt entreaty, I cannot bear that you should bring distinction only to our world of women and be rejected by society. That is why I have brought you here: to intoxicate you with numinous wine, steep you in immortal tea, warn you through marvellous songs, and then give you my younger sister in marriage. Her childhood name is Jian-mei, “Beauty Combined”, and her courtesy name Ke-qing.

‘Tonight is auspicious; you may marry at once. You need only learn that even this immortal bedchamber in an illusory realm offers no more than this. How much less, then, can the mortal world offer? Henceforth you must free yourself from these entanglements, awaken from your former passions, attend to Confucius and Mencius, and devote yourself to the work of governing the world.’ She then privately instructed him in the business of cloud and rain, pushed him into the room, closed the door and went away.

Still dazed, Bao-yu followed Disenchantment’s instructions, and the intimacies of lovers took their course, which cannot be fully recounted. By the next day he and Ke-qing were bound to each other in tender feeling and gentle words, unable to bear parting. As they went out hand in hand to amuse themselves, they suddenly came to a place overgrown with thorns and brambles, where wolves and tigers ran together. A black stream blocked their path, with no bridge across it. While they hesitated, Disenchantment came running up behind them. ‘Do not go any further! Turn back at once!’

Bao-yu stopped hurriedly. ‘What is this place?’ ‘This is the Ford of Delusion,’ Disenchantment said. ‘It is ten thousand zhang deep and stretches a thousand li. No boat can cross it. There is only a wooden raft: Layman Wood steers it and Attendant Ash poles it. They accept no gold or silver in thanks, but ferry across only those with whom they have a destined bond.

‘You have happened to wander here today. If you were to fall in, you would gravely betray all the earnest warnings I gave you.’ Before she had finished, the waters of the Ford of Delusion thundered, and a host of yakshas and sea-demons came to drag Bao-yu down. Sweat poured off him like rain; in terror he cried out, ‘Ke-qing, save me!’ Alarmed, Aroma and the other maids hurried to hold him. ‘Don’t be afraid, Bao-yu! We’re here!’

Now Qin-shi was outside the room, telling the little maids to keep a good watch in case the cats and dogs fought. Suddenly she heard Bao-yu call her childhood name in his dream. She wondered, ‘No one here has ever known my childhood name. How does he know it, to call it out in his sleep?’ As the saying goes:
In one deep dream, with whom am I made close?
Of lovers through the ages, I alone am so besotted.

Now Qin-shi, hearing Bao-yu call her childhood name in his dream, was naturally puzzled, but could hardly question him closely. Bao-yu himself was dazed, as though something had slipped away from him. The others hurried to bring him some longan soup. After sipping two mouthfuls, he got up to straighten his clothes. As Aroma reached to tie his trouser-sash, her hand happened to brush his thigh and felt a patch of cold dampness. Startled, she snatched it away and asked what had happened. Bao-yu flushed scarlet and gave her hand a squeeze.

Aroma was an intelligent girl, two years older than Bao-yu, and had lately begun to understand something of these matters. Seeing his condition, she guessed half the truth. She too blushed crimson with embarrassment and dared ask no more.

She finished putting his clothes in order, and they went to Grandmother Jia’s. After a hasty supper he came back to his own rooms. When the wet nurses and other maids were out of the way, Aroma hastily fetched him a fresh undergarment and helped him change.
‘Dear sister,’ Bao-yu pleaded, blushing, ‘whatever you do, don’t tell anyone.’
Blushing herself, Aroma asked with a smile, ‘What was it you dreamed about?
‘Where did all that dirty stuff come from?’
‘It’s a long story,’ Bao-yu said.

He told Aroma his dream in detail. When he came to the love of cloud and rain that Disenchantment had taught him, she hid her face and bent double, laughing with embarrassment. Bao-yu had always been fond of Aroma’s gentle, winning ways and her pretty looks, and now pressed her to join him in what Disenchantment had taught. Aroma had long known that Grandmother Jia had given her to Bao-yu, and felt that even now this would not be a breach of propriety. So they secretly tried it together; fortunately no one came upon them. From then on Bao-yu treated Aroma differently from all the others, and she served him with still greater devotion. For the moment there is nothing more to tell of them.

Taking the Rong household as a whole, there were not so very many people: three or four hundred, from highest to lowest. Nor were there so very many affairs: ten or twenty a day. Yet they were as tangled as a skein of hemp, with no end to catch hold of and draw into order.

Just as we were wondering which affair and which person would make the best beginning, there happened to come, from a thousand li away, a tiny household, insignificant as a mustard seed or a bean. Through a slight connection with the Rong family, members of it were on their way to the mansion that very day. This little household will therefore give us a thread to follow.

What was their surname? Who were they, and what connection did they have with the Rong mansion? If you gentlemen find such things petty and vulgar, put this book down at once and seek a better one to refresh your eyes. But if you think they may pass an idle hour, let this blockhead tell you all about them.

The little household just mentioned belonged to the Wang family, natives of the district. An ancestor had held a very minor post in the capital and had known Lady Wang’s father, Xi-feng’s grandfather. Coveting the influence and advantages of that family, he had claimed kinship through their shared surname and acknowledged himself a nephew. At the time, only Lady Wang and her eldest brother, Xi-feng’s father, had been living in the capital, so they alone knew of this branch of nominal relations; the others knew nothing of it. That ancestor was now dead. His only son, Wang Cheng, had seen the family fortunes decline and moved out of the city to their old village. Wang Cheng too had recently died of illness, leaving only his son, known by the childhood name Gou-er. Gou-er in turn had a son, called Ban-er, and his lawful wife, née Liu, had also borne him a daughter, Qing-er. This family of four still lived by farming. As Gou-er did other work during the day to earn a living, and his wife was busy drawing water, grinding grain and doing the housework, no one was left to look after the two siblings, Qing-er and Ban-er. Gou-er therefore brought his mother-in-law, Grannie Liu, to live with them. She was an old woman who had been widowed for many years, with no children at her side, subsisting on two mu of poor land.

Naturally she was glad to have her son-in-law take her in and support her, and she devoted herself to helping him and her daughter get by. It was the end of autumn, the beginning of winter. The weather was turning cold, and nothing had yet been got ready for the season. Gou-er could not help worrying. After a few cups of wine drunk to drown his troubles, he began finding things to rage about at home. His wife dared not answer back. Grannie Liu could bear it no longer.

‘Son-in-law,’ she said, ‘don’t be cross with me for speaking out. We country people live honestly, don’t we? We eat as much rice as our bowl will hold. When you were little, you had your old father to thank for easy eating and drinking, and now you can’t keep yourself in hand. When you have money, you think of today and never tomorrow; when it’s gone, you fly into a temper. Is that how a grown man behaves? We may live outside the city, but we’re still at the Son of Heaven’s feet. There’s money everywhere in Chang’an, only nobody knows how to pick it up. Jumping up and down at home won’t do any good.’
‘All you can do is talk nonsense from the kang!’ Gou-er burst out. ‘Do you want me to rob people or steal?’
‘Who’s telling you to steal?
‘We ought at least to put our heads together and think of something. You don’t suppose the money will come running to our house by itself?’

Gou-er gave a cold laugh. ‘If there were a way, would I have waited till now? I’ve no relations collecting taxes, no friends in office, no friends in office. What can I possibly think of? Even if I had any, I doubt they’d bother with us!’

‘That’s not necessarily so,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘We make the plans; Heaven decides whether they work. Once we’ve done our part, who knows? With the Bodhisattva’s blessing, a chance may come. In fact, I’ve thought of one for you. Your family used to claim kinship with the Wangs of Jinling. Twenty years ago they treated you well enough. It’s only because you’ve been so stiff-necked, refusing to go near them, that you’ve drifted apart. Your wife and I went there once, back then. The second daughter was a lively, open-handed girl, knew how to treat people and never put on airs. She’s now the wife of the Second Master Jia at the Rong mansion. I hear that as she’s grown older she’s become still kinder to the poor and the old. She loves feeding Buddhist monks, honouring Taoist priests, giving out rice and money. The Wang family may have gone off to a frontier appointment on promotion, but I dare say that married daughter would still remember us. Why don’t you pay her a visit? She may remember old times and do something for us. If she takes it into her head to be kind, a single hair plucked from her body would be thicker than our waists.’
His wife put in, ‘What you say is true, Mother, but how could people like you and me show our faces at her door?
‘To begin with, the gatekeepers might not even take in a message. We’d only go there to be snubbed and make fools of ourselves.’
Gou-er, however, cared more for advancement and gain than anything else, and the suggestion had begun to stir him. Hearing his wife’s objection, he smiled.
‘Since you say so, Grannie, and you’ve met the lady once before, why don’t you go yourself tomorrow and see which way the wind blows?’
‘Good heavens!’ said Grannie Liu. ‘There’s a saying: “A great lord’s gate is as deep as the sea.” What sort of creature am I? The people there don’t know me. I’d be going for nothing.’

‘Never mind,’ Gou-er said, smiling. ‘I’ll tell you how to manage it. Take your grandson Ban-er, and ask first for Zhou Rui, the servant she brought with her from her own family when she married. If you see him, you may get somewhere. Zhou Rui and my father once had a piece of business together. We’re on very good terms.’
‘I know him too,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘But it’s been so long since we saw anything of him. Who knows how he is now?

‘Well, there’s no help for it. You’re a man, and with that face of yours you plainly can’t go. My daughter’s a young married woman, and she can hardly go showing herself about. I’d better risk this old face of mine and try. If anything good comes of it, we’ll all benefit. And even if I bring back no money, I’ll have seen something of the world inside a duke’s or a marquis’s gates. My life won’t have been wasted.’
They all laughed at this, and that evening settled what was to be done.

Next day Grannie Liu rose before dawn to wash and comb her hair, and gave Ban-er a few instructions. The child was only five or six and understood nothing of it. Delighted to hear that his grandmother was taking him into town for an outing, he agreed to everything. She led him into the city and found her way to Ning-Rong Street. Before the stone lions at the Rong mansion’s main gate she saw such a crowd of sedan-chairs and horses that she dared go no further. She brushed down her clothes, gave Ban-er a few more instructions, then edged towards a side gate. Several men sat on a long bench, chests thrust out and bellies prominent, gesticulating as they talked of this and that. Grannie Liu had to sidle up to them.
‘Blessings upon you, masters.’
They looked her over for a while, then asked, ‘Where are you from?’
‘I’m looking for Master Zhou, Zhou Rui, Her Ladyship’s family servant,’ she said with an ingratiating smile. ‘Would one of you masters be so kind as to ask him to come out?’
They paid no attention. At length one said, ‘Go and wait over there by the corner of the wall. Someone from his household will be coming out presently.’

An older man among them said, ‘Don’t hold her up. Why make sport of her?’ He turned to Grannie Liu. ‘Master Zhou has gone south. His home’s in the row at the back, and his wife’s in. If you want her, go round this way to the street behind and ask at the back gate.’

Grannie Liu thanked him and led Ban-er round to the back gate. Hawkers had set down their carrying-poles outside, some selling food, others toys. Twenty or thirty children were romping about in a noisy crowd. Grannie Liu caught hold of one.
‘Let me ask you, young fellow: is Mrs Zhou at home?’
‘Which Mrs Zhou?’ the children asked.
‘We’ve three Mrs Zhous here, and two Mistress Zhous besides. Which sort is yours?’
‘Zhou Rui, Her Ladyship’s family servant.’
‘That’s easy. Follow me.’
Skipping and scampering, the child led Grannie Liu through the back gate to a courtyard wall and pointed.
‘That’s where she lives.’
Then he called, ‘Mrs Zhou! An old lady’s come to see you. I’ve brought her here.’
Hearing this, Zhou Rui’s wife hurried out.
‘Who is it?’
Grannie Liu stepped forward. ‘How are you, Sister Zhou?’
Zhou Rui’s wife stared for a while before recognising her, then smiled.
‘Grannie Liu! How are you? Tell me, how many years has it been? I’ve quite forgotten. Come in and sit down.’
‘An important person like you has so much to remember,’ Grannie Liu said, smiling as she went in. ‘How could you remember us?’
Inside, Zhou Rui’s wife told a young maid she employed to pour tea.
‘How you’ve grown!’ she said to Ban-er.
After asking about various things that had happened since they last met, she turned to Grannie Liu.
‘Were you passing today, or have you come specially?’
‘I came specially to see you, Sister, and to pay my respects to Her Ladyship as well. If you could take me to see her, so much the better. If not, I’ll rely on you to pass on my respects.’
Zhou Rui’s wife had already guessed something of her purpose.

Years before, when her husband had been competing to buy a piece of land, Gou-er had given him a great deal of help. Seeing Grannie Liu arrive like this, she could hardly refuse her. Besides, she wanted to display her own standing. At these words she smiled.
‘Don’t worry, Grannie. You’ve come all this way in good faith. Surely we can’t let you go without seeing the living Buddha herself?

‘Strictly speaking, receiving visitors and announcing them is nothing to do with me. Everyone here has a particular job. My husband only looks after the rents in spring and autumn. At other times all he has to do is go out with the young masters. My job is to attend the ladies when they go out. But since you’re a relation of Her Ladyship’s, and you’ve thought enough of me to come to me for help, I’ll make an exception and take in a message for you. There’s just one thing you don’t know, Grannie. This place isn’t what it was five years ago. Her Ladyship hardly attends to business now. Mrs Lian manages the household. Do you know who Mrs Lian is? Her Ladyship’s own niece, the daughter of her eldest brother, the one they used to call Feng.’
‘So it’s her!’ Grannie Liu exclaimed in surprise. ‘Well, no wonder. I said in those days she was a fine girl. Then I’ll get to see her today as well?’

‘Of course,’ said Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘Her Ladyship has so much to trouble her now that she passes on any visitor she can, and Miss Feng sees to them all. Even if you don’t see Her Ladyship today, you must see her, or your journey will have been wasted.’
‘Blessed Buddha! I’m entirely in your hands, Sister.’
‘Don’t say that. As the saying goes, “Make things easy for others and you make them easy for yourself.” It only costs me a word. What harm can it do me?’
She sent the young maid to the front hall to find out quietly whether the meal had been laid in Grandmother Jia’s rooms. The girl went off, and the two women talked of other things.
‘Miss Feng can’t be more than twenty this year,’ said Grannie Liu. ‘To be so capable, and manage a household like this! That’s something you don’t often see.’

‘Oh, Grannie, I couldn’t begin to tell you!’ said Zhou Rui’s wife. ‘Young as she is, she can outdo anyone in the way she handles things. She’s grown into a real beauty, and has ten thousand little ways about her, at the very least. As for arguing, ten clever-tongued men couldn’t get the better of her. You’ll believe me when you see her. There’s only one thing: she’s rather too hard on the servants.’
As they talked, the young maid returned.
‘The meal has been served in Her Old Ladyship’s rooms. Mrs Lian is with Her Ladyship.’
Zhou Rui’s wife got up at once and urged Grannie Liu to hurry.

‘Quick, quick! When she comes back to have her own meal, there’ll be a moment free. Let’s get there first. If we’re late, people will be coming to report on business and it’ll be hard to get a word in. Then she’ll have her nap, and there’ll be no time at all.’
They climbed down from the kang, brushed their clothes, gave Ban-er a few more instructions and followed Zhou Rui’s wife by a winding route towards Jia Lian’s quarters.

At the front hall Zhou Rui’s wife settled Grannie Liu to wait a little, then went past the screen wall and through the courtyard gate herself. Finding that Xi-feng had not yet returned, she first sought out Patience, one of Xi-feng’s trusted senior chamber-maids, who also shared her master’s bed. Zhou Rui’s wife explained who Grannie Liu was and how she came to be there.

‘She’s come all this way today specially to pay her respects. Her Ladyship used to see her often, so we really couldn’t refuse to see her today. That’s why I’ve brought her in. When the mistress comes back, I’ll explain it all. I don’t think she’ll blame me for taking too much on myself.’
Patience made the decision.
‘Bring them in. They can sit here for the time being.’

Only then did Zhou Rui’s wife go out and bring the two of them into the courtyard. They mounted the steps of the main rooms, and a young maid lifted a scarlet felt curtain. As soon as they entered the central room, a wave of fragrance struck Grannie Liu’s face. She could not tell what scent it was and felt as though she were floating among clouds. Everything in the room glittered and shone, dazzling her eyes and making her head swim. All she could do was nod, click her tongue and invoke the Buddha.

They went into the room on the east, where Jia Lian’s little daughter, Da-jie, slept. Patience stood by the edge of the kang, looked Grannie Liu over once or twice, then greeted her and offered her a seat. Seeing Patience dressed from head to foot in fine silks, wearing gold and silver, with a face as lovely as flowers and jade, Grannie Liu took her for Xi-feng. She was just about to address her as ‘Madam’ when she heard Zhou Rui’s wife call her ‘Miss Patience’, and Patience in turn address the other woman as ‘Mrs Zhou’. Only then did she realise that this was merely a maid of some standing. Grannie Liu and Ban-er were invited up on to the kang; Patience and Zhou Rui’s wife sat facing each other on its edge. A young maid poured tea for them.
Just as she was about to ask, the young maids all began running about, saying, ‘The mistress is back.’
Zhou Rui’s wife and Patience rose hurriedly.
‘Just wait here,’ they told Grannie Liu. ‘We’ll come and fetch you when it’s time.’
With that they went out to meet her.

Grannie Liu waited without a sound, her head tilted to listen. Laughter came from a distance, and some ten or twenty women, their clothes and skirts rustling, gradually entered the central room and went into the room on the other side. Two or three more women came into the room where she sat, carrying large lacquered food-boxes, and waited. From the other side came the command, ‘Serve the meal.’ Little by little the crowd withdrew, leaving only the few who were serving the dishes.

After a long spell of utter silence, two people appeared carrying a low kang-table and set it on the kang beside her. It was thickly covered with bowls and dishes still full of fish and meat; only a few had been touched. Ban-er clamoured for meat as soon as he saw it, and Grannie Liu slapped him away. Just then Zhou Rui’s wife came over, all smiles, and beckoned to her. Understanding the signal, Grannie Liu brought Ban-er down from the kang and into the central room. Zhou Rui’s wife whispered to her for a little while before taking her into the other room.

A soft scarlet curtain scattered with flowers hung at the doorway from chased copper hooks. Beneath the south window stood a kang spread with a strip of scarlet felt. Against the wooden partition on the east were a backrest of chain-patterned brocade and a bolster. A large seat-cushion was covered in satin shimmering gold and green; beside it stood a carved-lacquer spittoon.

Xi-feng was dressed informally in a Zhaojun hood of autumn sable, encircled by a band of clustered pearls. She wore a peach-red jacket scattered with flowers, a dark-blue silk-tapestry cloak lined with grey squirrel, and a scarlet foreign-crêpe skirt lined with ermine. Bright with powder and rouge, she sat perfectly upright, stirring the ashes in her hand-warmer with a little pair of copper tongs. Patience stood at the edge of the kang holding a small tea tray decorated with filled-in lacquer, with a little covered teacup on it. Xi-feng neither took the tea nor raised her head, but went on stirring the ashes.
‘Why haven’t they been asked in yet?’ she said slowly.
As she spoke, she lifted herself to take the tea and saw that Zhou Rui’s wife had already brought two people in. They were standing on the floor before her.

She at once made as if to rise but, before actually doing so, greeted them with a face all smiles and reproached Zhou Rui’s wife for not telling her sooner. Grannie Liu had already bowed several times from where she stood.
‘My respects to you, Madam.’

‘Sister Zhou, quick, help her up. No more bowing,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Please sit down. I’m young and don’t know all our relations. I’m not sure which generation you belong to, so I daren’t venture on a form of address.’
‘This is the grannie I was telling you about,’ Zhou Rui’s wife hastened to explain.
Xi-feng nodded. Grannie Liu was now sitting on the edge of the kang, with Ban-er hiding behind her. No amount of coaxing could persuade him to come out and bow.

‘When relations seldom visit, they drift apart,’ Xi-feng said with a smile. ‘Those who know the circumstances say you’ve taken a dislike to us and won’t come. But spiteful people who don’t know may think we look down on everyone.’
Grannie Liu hurried to invoke the Buddha.
‘We’re badly off. We can’t afford to make visits. If we came here, we’d only bring shame on you, Madam. Even your stewards would think we looked out of place.’

‘That’s a dreadful thing to say,’ Xi-feng replied, smiling. ‘We only live on our grandfather’s empty reputation and a poorly paid official post. What has any of us got? Just an empty shell left over from the old days. As the saying goes, “Even the imperial court has three branches of poor relations.” How much more must you and I?’
She asked Zhou Rui’s wife whether she had informed Lady Wang.
‘I was waiting for your instructions, ma’am.’
‘Go and see. If she has someone with her on business, leave it. If she’s free, tell her and see what she says.’

Zhou Rui’s wife assented and went. Xi-feng had someone bring a handful of fruit for Ban-er, and had just begun to ask a few casual questions when a number of married women servants with household duties arrived to report on business. Patience announced them.
‘I have a visitor,’ said Xi-feng. ‘Let them come back this evening. If anything is very urgent, bring them in and I’ll deal with it now.’
Patience went out and presently returned.
‘I’ve asked them all. There was nothing urgent, so I sent them away.’
Xi-feng nodded. Zhou Rui’s wife came back and addressed her.

‘Her Ladyship says she has no time today. If you keep them company, ma’am, it will be just the same. She thanks them for thinking of her. If they’ve simply come for a visit, very well. If there’s anything they want to say, they should tell you. It will be just the same.’

Jia Rong grinned and, kneeling on one knee on the edge of the kang, pleaded with her.

‘You have just the same things at home. You’re never content once you’ve seen mine.’
‘Nothing there is as good as this,’ Jia Rong said with a smile. ‘Do be merciful!’
‘If you so much as chip it, look out for your skin!’
She told Patience to get the key to the upstairs rooms and send a few reliable people to carry it over. Jia Rong’s whole face lit up.

‘Rong, come back!’ she called through the window.
Several voices outside took up the call. ‘Master Rong, come back at once!’
Jia Rong hurried back and stood with his hands at his sides, waiting for her instructions.
Xi-feng merely went on sipping her tea, lost in thought for a long while. Then she smiled.

Jia Rong assented and slowly withdrew.

‘I’ve brought your nephew today for nothing else but this: his father and mother at home haven’t even anything to eat. And now it’s turned cold. However much we think, we can see no way out. So I had to bring your nephew and come to you.’

Xi-feng had long since understood. Hearing how poorly she put it, she stopped her with a smile.

If there’s anything they want to say, you’re to decide what’s best, ma’am.’
‘That explains it,’ said Xi-feng. ‘I wondered how they could be relations without my having the faintest idea who they were.’

‘Ah, I know what difficulties are. But as they say, “Even a camel starved to death is bigger than a horse.” Whatever happens, a single hair plucked from your body is thicker than our waists!’
Finding her language coarse, Zhou Rui’s wife kept signalling with her eyes for her to stop.

As she spoke, she stood up.

‘Good heavens, Grannie! Why did you forget how to talk as soon as you saw her? The first words out of your mouth were “your nephew”.

‘Oh, Sister,’ Grannie Liu said, laughing, ‘I liked her so much the moment I saw her, I couldn’t find the words.’

Zhou Rui’s wife thought nothing of such a sum and firmly refused it. Grannie Liu could not thank her enough, and left again by the back gate. As the saying goes:
When fortune is at its height, a helping hand comes easily;
A deeply felt kindness binds more closely than kin or friends.

‘Is Cousin Bao-chai quite well again?’

‘Yes, indeed. And you were kind enough to send someone to ask after her the other day. She’s in the inner room. Go and see her. It’s warmer in there than here. Sit there, and I’ll come and talk to you when I’ve put these things in order.’

Bao-yu climbed down from the kang and went to the inner doorway, where a soft curtain of somewhat worn red silk hung. Lifting it and stepping inside, he saw Xue Bao-chai sitting on the kang at her needlework. Her glossy black hair was coiled in a bun. She wore a honey-coloured padded jacket, a rose-purple sleeveless coat worked in two shades of gold and lined with ermine, and a padded skirt of spring-onion-yellow figured silk. None of her clothes was quite new or old, and there was nothing ostentatious about her appearance.

Her lips were red without rouge, her brows dark without being painted. Her face was round as a silver basin, her eyes like glistening apricots. She spoke little, which people called hiding her simplicity; she kept her place and accommodated herself to circumstances, which she herself called keeping to her unassuming ways. As Bao-yu looked at her, he asked, ‘Are you quite well again, Cousin?’
Bao-chai looked up and saw him coming in. She rose at once and answered with a smile, ‘Much better now. Thank you for thinking of me.’

She invited him to sit on the edge of the kang and told Oriole to pour tea. While asking after Grandmother, her aunt and the other girls, she looked at Bao-yu. On his head was a purple-gold filigree coronet set with jewels, and across his forehead a gold band with two dragons contending for a pearl. He wore an olive-yellow robe with upright python patterns, close-fitting archer’s sleeves and a lining of white fox underarm fur. At his waist was a five-coloured sash with a butterfly design. Round his neck hung a longevity locket and an amulet of religious dedication, as well as the precious jade that had been in his mouth when he was born.
‘I hear about this jade of yours every day,’ Bao-chai said with a smile, ‘but I’ve never really had a good look at it. Today I mean to.’
She moved closer.

Bao-yu moved towards her too, took it from his neck and put it in her hand. As Bao-chai held it on her palm, she saw that it was the size of a sparrow’s egg, brilliant as radiant sunset clouds, smooth and lustrous as cream, with patterns of five colours winding round it. This was the guise assumed by that unhewn stone beneath Green Ridge Peak on the Mountain of Great Desolation. A later poet once mocked it in these lines:

Nüwa smelting stones was wild enough a tale;
From that wild tale unfolds the Great Desolation.

It lost the true realm of the hidden spirit,
To take this phantom shape beside a stinking bag of flesh.

Know that when fortune fails, gold loses colour;
Lament that when the times go wrong, jade cannot shine.

White bones lie mountain-high, their surnames lost:
Nothing but noble youths and girls in crimson dress.

The stone had also recorded this transformed appearance and the seal-script inscriptions engraved by the scabby monk. These are reproduced below according to its drawing. Its actual body was tiny, small enough to be held in the mouth of a child emerging from the womb. Were we to draw it at its true size, the writing would be so minute that readers would have to strain their eyes, which would hardly be agreeable. We have therefore kept only the shape and enlarged the proportions a little, so that it may be read by lamplight or when tipsy. By explaining this now, we forestall such objections as: ‘How large can an unborn child’s mouth be, to hold such a huge, clumsy lump?’
Spiritual Jade: Front
Spiritual Jade
Never lose, never forget
Immortal life, enduring prosperity
Spiritual Jade: Reverse
1. Banishes evil influences
2. Cures grievous afflictions
3. Discerns fortune and misfortune
When she had finished looking, Bao-chai turned it over to examine the front again and read aloud: ‘Never lose, never forget; Immortal life, enduring prosperity.’
After reading it twice, she turned to Oriole with a smile.
‘Why are you standing here in a daze instead of pouring the tea?’
Oriole giggled. ‘Those two lines sound as though they make a pair with the two on your necklace, miss.’
‘So you have eight characters on your necklace too, Cousin!’ Bao-yu exclaimed, smiling. ‘Let me admire them as well.’
‘Don’t listen to her,’ said Bao-chai. ‘There’s no writing on it.’
‘Dear Cousin,’ Bao-yu pleaded with a smile, ‘why did you look at mine, then?’

Unable to resist his pestering, Bao-chai said, ‘Someone gave us a couple of auspicious sayings, so they were engraved on it, and I was told to wear it every day. Otherwise, what pleasure is there in carrying such a weight?’

As she spoke, she undid the row of buttons and drew out from over her scarlet inner jacket a jewelled necklace, its gems glittering and its gold ablaze. Bao-yu promptly took the locket in his hand. Sure enough, there were four seal-script characters on each side, eight altogether, forming two auspicious pronouncements.

Its appearance, too, had been drawn to show the design. The front of the necklace bore, in ordinary transcription: ‘Never part, never forsake.’ The reverse bore: ‘Youth and beauty, ever renewed.’ Bao-yu read these twice, then read his own twice.
‘These eight characters of yours really do make a pair with mine, Cousin,’ he said with a smile.
‘They were given by a scabby-headed monk,’ said Oriole, smiling. ‘He said they had to be engraved on something made of gold—’

Before she could finish, Bao-chai reproved her for not pouring the tea and asked Bao-yu where he had come from. Sitting so close to her, Bao-yu kept catching a delicate scent, sweet and cool, whose nature he could not make out.
‘What incense have you been using on your clothes, Cousin?
‘I’ve never smelt anything like it.’
‘I can’t bear perfuming clothes,’ Bao-chai said with a smile. ‘Perfectly good clothes, and you make them all smoky and singed-smelling.’
‘Then what is this scent?’ Bao-yu asked.
Bao-chai thought a moment, then smiled. ‘Of course. It must be the pill I took this morning.’
‘What sort of pill smells so lovely?’ Bao-yu asked with a smile. ‘Dear Cousin, give me one to taste.’
‘There you go again,’ she said, smiling. ‘Do you think medicines are things to take just as you please?’
She had hardly finished when someone outside announced, ‘Miss Lin is here.’ Before the words were out, Lin Dai-yu came swaying gracefully into the room. At sight of Bao-yu she smiled.
‘Oh dear, I’ve chosen a bad moment!’
Bao-yu and the others rose at once, smiling and inviting her to sit down.
‘What makes you say that?’ Bao-chai asked with a smile.
‘If I’d known he was coming, I wouldn’t have come,’ Dai-yu said, smiling.
‘Now I understand you even less.’

‘Either everyone comes in a crowd, or nobody comes at all. If he comes today and I come tomorrow, and we take turns like that, won’t you have someone here every day? Then you won’t be too lonely, or have too much company either. How is it you don’t understand, Cousin?’
Seeing that Dai-yu wore a scarlet camlet coat fastening down the front, Bao-yu asked, ‘Is it snowing?’
‘Snow pellets have been falling for quite a while,’ the women standing below the kang replied.
‘Has anyone brought my cloak?’ Bao-yu asked.
‘There, you see,’ said Dai-yu. ‘As soon as I come, it’s time for you to go.’
‘When did I say I was going?’ Bao-yu laughed. ‘I only want it here in case I need it.’
His wet-nurse, Nurse Li, said, ‘It’s snowing, and getting rather late. You might as well stay here and amuse yourself with your cousins.
‘Your aunt is laying out tea and refreshments. I’ll send a maid for your cloak and tell the pages they can go.’

Bao-yu agreed. Nurse Li went out and dismissed the pages, of whom no more need be said. Aunt Xue had set out several dainty things to eat and was keeping her visitors to tea. Bao-yu praised the delicious goose feet and duck tongues he had eaten at Cousin Zhen’s wife’s in the other mansion the other day. Aunt Xue promptly brought him some of her own, preserved in wine lees, to taste.
‘These really need wine with them,’ Bao-yu said with a smile.
Aunt Xue sent for some of the very best wine.
Nurse Li came forward. ‘Madam, perhaps no wine.’
‘Mamma, just one cup,’ Bao-yu pleaded.

‘No, that won’t do! In front of Her Old Ladyship or Her Ladyship, I wouldn’t mind if you drank a whole jar. But the other day I took my eyes off you for a moment, and some ill-bred creature, thinking only of pleasing you and not caring what happened to anyone else, gave you a sip of wine. I was scolded for two days because of it. You don’t know, madam, what an aggravating temper he has. Wine only makes him more wilful. One day Her Old Ladyship is in a good mood and lets him drink as much as he likes; another day she won’t let him touch it. Why should I suffer for nothing in between?’
‘You old thing,’ Aunt Xue said, laughing, ‘go and have a drink yourself, and stop worrying.
‘I shan’t let him have too much either. If Her Old Ladyship asks, I’ll answer for it.’
She told a young maid, ‘Come, see that your mammas have a cup too, to keep out the snowy chill.’
Hearing this, Nurse Li could only go with the others to have some wine. Bao-yu now said, ‘There’s no need to warm it. I only like it cold.’
‘That will never do,’ Aunt Xue said at once. ‘Cold wine makes your hand shake when you write.’

Bao-chai smiled. ‘Cousin Bao, with all the odds and ends you pick up every day, surely you know that wine is intensely heating by nature? Drink it warm and it disperses quickly. Drink it cold and it congeals inside you, and your five internal organs have to warm it. How can that fail to do harm? Do give up drinking it cold.’
Bao-yu thought this reasonable. He put down the cold wine and had it warmed before drinking.
Dai-yu sat cracking melon seeds, with only a close-lipped smile. Just then her little maid Snowgoose brought her a small hand-warmer.
‘Who told you to bring that?’ Dai-yu asked, smiling. ‘How very thoughtful! As though I were about to freeze to death!’
‘Nightingale was afraid you’d be cold, miss, and sent me with it,’ Snowgoose replied.
Dai-yu took it and clasped it to her bosom.
‘How good of you to listen to her!’ she said, smiling. ‘Everything I say to you goes in one ear and out the other. Why is it that when she speaks, you obey faster than if it were an imperial decree?’
Bao-yu knew she was using this to make fun of him, but could think of nothing to say in reply. He merely gave a couple of little laughs. Bao-chai knew Dai-yu’s ways of old and took no notice.
‘You’ve always been delicate,’ Aunt Xue said. ‘You can’t stand the cold. Is it wrong of them to think of you?’

‘You don’t understand, Aunt,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘It’s fortunate I’m here with you. If it were someone else’s house, mightn’t they be offended? It looks as though I thought they couldn’t even provide a hand-warmer, so I had to have one specially sent from home. Instead of saying my maids are over-anxious, they would think I was always so ill-mannered and presumptuous.’
‘You do imagine things!’ Aunt Xue said. ‘You may think of that, but I never would.’

During this conversation Bao-yu had already drunk three cups. Nurse Li came forward to stop him again. He was feeling thoroughly content, talking and laughing with Bao-chai and Dai-yu. How could he be willing to stop? He had to swallow his pride and plead.
‘Dear Mamma, just two more cups, and then no more.’
‘Mind yourself,’ said Nurse Li. ‘The Master is at home today. He may ask you about your books!’
This made Bao-yu thoroughly uneasy. He slowly put down his wine and lowered his head. Dai-yu spoke at once.
‘Don’t spoil everyone’s fun! If Uncle sends for you, just say Aunt is keeping you here. This mamma has had a drink herself, and now she wants to amuse herself at our expense!’
She gave Bao-yu a secret nudge to stir him to defiance, and murmured, ‘Don’t mind the old thing. Let’s enjoy ourselves.’
Nurse Li knew Dai-yu’s ways too.
‘Miss Lin, don’t encourage him. Do try to persuade him. He might listen to you.’

‘Why should I encourage him?’ Dai-yu said with a cold laugh. ‘And I’ve no call to persuade him either. You’re far too anxious, Mamma. Grandmother often gives him wine. Surely an extra mouthful here at Aunt’s can’t hurt him. Unless, of course, Aunt is an outsider, and perhaps he oughtn’t to be here at all.’
Nurse Li was both flustered and amused.
‘Really, Miss Lin! Every word you say is sharper than a knife. Where does all that come into it?’
Bao-chai could not help laughing either. She pinched Dai-yu’s cheek.
‘That mouth of yours, Pin-pin! One hardly knows whether to be cross with you or love you.’
Aunt Xue put in, ‘Don’t be afraid, my boy, don’t be afraid!

‘I’ve nothing very good to offer you when you come here. If you’re frightened into letting even this little bit lie heavy on your stomach, you’ll make me feel bad. Go on and enjoy it. I’ll answer for everything. Stay for supper too. If you get drunk, you can sleep here with me.’
She gave orders: ‘Warm some more wine! I’ll have a couple of cups with you, and then we’ll eat.’
Only then did Bao-yu’s spirits rise again.
‘Who knows how they may be looking for us over there?’

With that, the two took their leave. A young maid brought his rain-hat. Bao-yu inclined his head a little and told her to put it on. She shook out the scarlet felt hat and had only just set it on his head when he protested.
‘Stop, stop! Clumsy thing, be a little gentler! Haven’t you ever seen anyone put one on? Let me do it myself.’
Dai-yu stood on the edge of the kang.
‘What a fuss! Come here and let me see.’

Bao-yu went over at once. Dai-yu adjusted the hat with her hands, settling it gently over the coronet that held his hair and tucking its brim above his forehead band. She raised the walnut-sized crimson floss tassel on his hairpin so that it quivered outside the hat. When she had finished she looked him over.
‘There. Now put your cloak on.’
Only then did Bao-yu take the cloak and put it on.
‘Your nurses haven’t come back yet,’ Aunt Xue said hastily. ‘There’s no hurry. Wait a little.’
‘Why should we wait for them?’ said Bao-yu. ‘The maids are quite enough to go with us.’
Aunt Xue was uneasy and would not be satisfied until she had ordered two women to accompany the cousins.

The two thanked her for her hospitality and went straight back to Grandmother Jia’s rooms. She had not yet had supper, and was all the more pleased when she heard they had come from Aunt Xue’s. Seeing that Bao-yu had been drinking, she sent him to rest in his room and forbade him to come out again. She ordered that he be carefully looked after. Then, remembering his attendants, she asked, ‘Where is Li, his wet-nurse?’
No one dared say she had gone home. ‘She was here just now,’ they answered. ‘She must have gone off on some errand.’
Bao-yu staggered and turned his head. ‘She has an easier life than you do, Grandmother. What do you want with her? I might live a couple of days longer without her.’
Talking as he went, he reached his bedroom. Brush and ink were on the table. Skybright came forward to meet him, smiling.

‘Well, well! You made me grind all that ink, and in your fine mood this morning you wrote just three characters, threw down the brush and went off. You’ve kept us waiting all day. Come and use up the ink before you do anything else!’
Bao-yu suddenly remembered what had happened that morning.
‘Where are the three characters I wrote?’ he asked with a smile.
‘He really is drunk!’ Skybright said, laughing.

‘Before you went to the other mansion, you told us to put them up over this doorway. Now you ask that! I was afraid someone else would spoil them, so I climbed the ladder and put them up myself. My hands are still stiff with cold.’
‘I forgot,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘If your hands are cold, let me warm them.’
He reached out and took her hand, and they looked up together at the three freshly written characters above the doorway. Presently Dai-yu came in.
‘Dear Cousin, tell me honestly,’ Bao-yu said with a smile. ‘Which of those three characters is best?’
Dai-yu looked up at the three characters newly pasted above the inner doorway. They read ‘Crimson Rue Studio’.
‘They’re all good,’ Dai-yu said with a smile. ‘How have you come to write so beautifully? You must write a name-board for me tomorrow.’
‘You’re coaxing me again,’ Bao-yu chuckled. Then he asked, ‘Where’s Aroma?’
Skybright pointed with her lips towards the kang in the inner room. Bao-yu looked and saw Aroma lying there asleep, still dressed.

‘Well, that’s rather early to be tucked up so snugly,’ he said with a smile. Then he asked Skybright, ‘At breakfast in the other mansion today there was a plate of bean-curd-skin parcels. I remembered you liked them, so I spoke to Mrs Zhen. I just said I wanted to keep them for tonight, and had someone send them over. Did you eat them?’

‘Don’t speak of it. As soon as they came I knew they were for me. But I’d only just eaten, so I put them aside. Then Mamma Li came and saw them. “Bao-yu probably won’t eat these,” she said. “I’ll take them for my grandson.” And she had someone carry them home.’
Just then Snowpink brought in the tea.
‘Have some tea, Cousin Lin,’ Bao-yu said.
The others laughed. ‘Miss Lin left some time ago, and you’re still offering her tea!’

Bao-yu drank half a bowl. Suddenly he remembered the morning’s tea and asked Snowpink, ‘There was a bowl of Maple Dew tea brewed this morning. I said it only comes into its own after three or four infusions. Why have you brewed this instead?’
‘I did keep it,’ said Snowpink. ‘But when Mamma Li came, she wanted to taste it, so I gave it to her.’
At this Bao-yu flung the cup he was holding straight to the floor.
It shattered with a crash, splashing tea all over Snowpink’s skirt. He sprang up and demanded of her:

‘What sort of mamma is she to you, for you all to be so dutiful? All she has to go on is that I drank her milk for a few days when I was little. Now you’ve let her set herself up above my ancestors. I don’t need her milk any more. Why keep an ancestor here doing nothing? Turn her out, and we’ll all have some peace!’
He was about to go that very instant and ask Grandmother Jia to dismiss his wet-nurse.

Aroma, in fact, had not been asleep at all. She had only pretended, to tempt Bao-yu into coming to tease her. When she first heard the talk about the writing and the parcels, there had been no need to get up. But when he smashed the teacup and lost his temper, she quickly rose to explain matters and soothe him. Grandmother Jia had already sent someone to ask what had happened.
‘I was bringing in the tea just now,’ Aroma said quickly, ‘and slipped on the snow. The cup fell out of my hand and broke.’

Then she tried to calm Bao-yu. ‘Very well, if you’ve set your heart on turning her out. We’d all like to go too. You might as well turn us all out together. It would suit us, and you needn’t worry about finding better people to wait on you.’

This silenced Bao-yu at last. Aroma and the others helped him to the kang and changed his clothes. They could not make out what he was still saying: his tongue was growing thick, his eyelids heavier and heavier. They hurried to settle him to sleep. Aroma took the Spiritual Jade from his neck, wrapped it in her own handkerchief and tucked it under the mattress, so that it would not chill his neck when he put it on next morning.

Bao-yu fell asleep as soon as his head touched the pillow. Nurse Li and the others had come back by then. Hearing that he was drunk, they dared not come forward and provoke him further. They quietly made sure he was asleep before dispersing, relieved. When he woke next day, someone reported that Master Rong from the other mansion had brought Master Qin to call. Bao-yu hurried out to welcome them and took Qin Zhong to pay his respects to Grandmother Jia. Delighted by the boy’s good looks and gentle manners, she thought him a worthy companion for Bao-yu’s studies. She kept him to tea and a meal, and had him taken to see Lady Wang and the others. They had always been fond of Qin-shi, and seeing what a fine boy Qin Zhong was, they too were pleased. Each gave him a gift when he left. Grandmother Jia gave him a purse and a gold figure of Kui Xing, to signify ‘harmony under the star of learning’. She also told him:

‘You live a long way off. If ever the heat or cold, or getting your meals, makes things awkward, stay here. There’s no need for a fixed rule. Just keep company with your Uncle Bao, and don’t learn the ways of those good-for-nothing creatures.’
Qin Zhong assented to each instruction, then went home and told his father.

His father, Qin Ye, currently held office as a secretary for building works. He was nearly seventy, and his wife had long been dead. Having had no children in his earlier years, he had adopted a boy and a girl from a foundling home. The boy had died, leaving only the girl, whose childhood name was Ke-er. She grew into a slender, graceful young woman with a charming disposition. Qin Ye had some longstanding connections with the Jias, and a marriage was arranged: she was betrothed to Jia Rong. Qin Ye was over fifty before Qin Zhong was born. The boy’s tutor had died the previous year, and there had been no opportunity to engage another accomplished teacher, so for the time being he had been reviewing his old lessons at home. Qin Ye had been thinking of approaching his daughter’s family by marriage about sending him to their school, so that his studies would not be neglected in the meantime, when this chance encounter with Bao-yu occurred. He knew too that the Jia school was now in the charge of Jia Dai-ru, a venerable scholar of the day. Qin Zhong was bound to improve there, and might hope to make a name for himself. Qin Ye was therefore delighted. His official purse, however, was poorly filled, and everyone in the Jia household, high and low, had eyes only for wealth and rank. A modest sum would hardly do, yet he feared harming his son’s prospects for life. There was nothing for it but to scrape together twenty-four taels, respectfully wrap them as an introductory gift to the teacher and take Qin Zhong himself to pay a call at Dai-ru’s house.
After that they waited to hear which day Bao-yu would begin school, so that the two could start together. As the saying has it:
Had they known the idle quarrels that would follow,
Would they have set out now to study on so false a path?

segments.text: Early on the appointed morning, when Bao-yu woke, Aroma had already packed his books, brushes and other writing things, putting everything neatly in order, and was sitting disconsolately on the edge of his bed. Seeing him awake, she had to help him wash and do his hair. Bao-yu noticed her gloomy look and asked with a smile, ‘Dear sister, what’s troubling you again? Surely you don’t blame me for going to school and leaving you all lonely?’

‘What a thing to say!’ Aroma said, smiling. ‘Studying is an excellent thing. You can’t drift along all your life. Where would that end? There’s only one thing: when you’re studying, keep your mind on your books, and when you’re not, spare a thought for home. Don’t go fooling about with the others. If your father catches you, it will be no laughing matter. Of course you want to work hard and do well, but it would be better to take on a little less. For one thing, if you bite off too much you can’t chew it, and for another, you must look after your health. That’s all I mean. Do try to understand.’
Bao-yu agreed to everything she said, point by point.

I’ve sent out charcoal for your foot-warmer and hand-warmer as well. You must make them keep those filled. By now he was fully dressed, and Aroma urged him to go and pay his respects to Grandmother Jia, Jia Zheng, Lady Wang and the others. segments.text: As luck would have it, Jia Zheng had come home rather early that day and was in the study chatting with his literary dependants. Bao-yu suddenly appeared, paid his respects and said he was going to school.

‘If you mention the word “school” again, you’ll make even me die of shame,’ Jia Zheng said with a cold laugh. ‘If you take my advice, you’ll simply go and play. That’s what you’re fit for. Mind you don’t soil my floor by standing on it, or my door by leaning against it!’
The literary gentlemen had all risen and were smiling.

‘Come, sir, why speak like that? Once our young friend starts today, in two or three years he’ll have made a name for himself. He certainly won’t go on behaving like a child as he did before. It’s nearly time for the morning meal. Do be on your way, young sir.’
Two of the older men took Bao-yu out by the hand.

segments.text: ‘You go to school with him every day,’ he said to Li Gui. ‘What books has he actually read? All he’s filled his head with is gossip and nonsense, and all he’s learnt is ever more elaborate mischief. When I have a moment to spare, I’ll flay you first and settle with that good-for-nothing afterwards!’

Terrified, Li Gui dropped on both knees, took off his cap and knocked his head audibly on the floor, saying ‘Yes, sir’ over and over. Then he ventured, ‘The young master’s got as far as the third volume of the Book of Poetry. Something about “The deer go yoo-yoo, lotus leaves and duckweed.” I wouldn’t dare lie, sir.’
The whole room burst out laughing. Even Jia Zheng could not help joining in.

‘He might read thirty volumes of the Book of Poetry, and it would still be like stopping his ears to steal a bell: nothing but an attempt to fool people. Go and give my respects to the old gentleman at the school. Tell him I said there is no need to go through the motions with the Book of Poetry or classical prose or any of that. What matters most is to explain the Four Books straight through first and have him learn them thoroughly by heart.’

After that Tealeaf dared not say another word.

segments.text: By this time Jia Rui too was afraid of the affair growing bigger. His own hands were far from clean, so he had to swallow his pride and plead first with Qin Zhong and then with Bao-yu. At first neither would give way. Eventually Bao-yu said, ‘Very well, I needn’t go home. Just make Jin Rong apologise, and that will do.’
Jin Rong refused at first, but could not hold out when Jia Rui began pressing him to apologise as well. Li Gui and the others had to coax him.
‘You started it, after all. How else can it be settled?’

Unable to resist any longer, Jin Rong bowed to Qin Zhong with clasped hands. Bao-yu was still not satisfied: he insisted on a kowtow. Jia Rui wanted only to quiet the affair for the moment. He took Jin Rong aside and urged him in a whisper, ‘As the saying goes, “Even an execution ends with a head touching the ground.” You’ve made the trouble, so you’ll have to swallow a little pride. One kowtow, and it’s over.’
Jin Rong had no choice. He went forward and kowtowed to Qin Zhong. For what followed, listen to the next chapter.
